abstract: We consider the problem of learning compositional robot policies end-to-end from expert demonstrations, without any pre-specified notion of task decomposition or hierarchy. We ask whether a VLA trained with a simplified Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) action head can emergently learn to decompose tasks into reusable, interpretable primitives. We find that learned experts are heavily reused across tasks and consistently correspond to qualitatively distinct low-level behaviors, suggesting that the router implicitly learns to perform high-level sequencing while experts serve as compositional primitives. Our MoE matches the task performance of a monolithic baseline while demonstrating meaningful expert specialization, a step toward modular, interpretable robot policies that emerge from data alone.
notes: Moderate — MoE architecture for compositional VLA skills; ICML workshop paper with limited scope

title: Safe Execution of RL Policies via Acceleration-based CBF-QP Constraint Enforcement for Real-World Robotic Deployments
authors: Bastien Muraccioli, Alice Cariou, Pierre-Alexandre Leziart, Mathieu Celerier, Arnaud Demont, Gentiane Venture, Mehdi Benallegue
matched_interests: Control Barrier Functions (CBFs)|Safe & robust robot control|Reinforcement learning
headline: CBF-QP safety filter cuts real humanoid RL constraint violations by 92%
summary: Introduces Acc-CBF-QP, an acceleration-based QP safety filter using CBFs that constrains any RL policy at runtime without modifying training. Tested on a 7-DoF Kinova Gen3 manipulator and 19-DoF Unitree H1 humanoid, achieving 92% reduction in constraint violations on real H1 hardware while preserving task performance.
abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has demonstrated remarkable capabilities for solving complex robotic control problems, but its lack of safety guarantees severely limits deployment on hardware. In particular, as legged robots and manipulators often operate near safety-critical boundaries, out-of-distribution states can lead to failure upon deployment. To address this, we introduce Acc-CBF-QP, an acceleration-based Quadratic Program (QP) safety filter using Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) that constrains any RL policy onto a safe set at runtime without modifying training. The method applies to unconstrained and Safe-RL policies, and enforces joint position, velocity, torque, and collision constraints within a unified optimization framework. A key contribution is the formulation of RL+QP tasks that regulate deviation from the RL command when constraints would otherwise be violated. We introduce a TorqueTask, minimizing torque deviation, and a Forward Dynamics Task, minimizing induced acceleration deviation, thus providing principled control over safety-performance trade-offs. Experiments on a 7-DoF Kinova Gen3 manipulator and a 19-DoF Unitree H1 humanoid, both in simulation and on hardware, highlight substantial reductions in constraint violations. On the real H1 hardware, a Safe-RL policy alone yielded 10.04 violations/s, which were reduced by 92% to 0.80 violations/s when augmented with Acc-CBF-QP. On the Kinova Gen3, Acc-CBF-QP fully eliminated violations. Nominal task performance of the RL objective is preserved in violation-free regimes. Under aggressive velocity commands on H1, Acc-CBF-QP improves execution by preventing constraint-induced shutdowns, yielding longer survival times. The full pipeline is open-source.
notes: High — CBF-based safety filter for RL policies on real humanoid and manipulator hardware (IROS 2026)

title: Lagrangian Perturbation Diffusion Steering: Latent Reinforcement Learning for Generative Policies
authors: Hikmet Simsir, Ozgur S. Oguz
headline: Lightweight RL adaptation of frozen diffusion policies via Lagrangian noise-space perturbation
summary: Proposes LP-DS, a lightweight method that improves frozen generative policies by learning compact noise-space perturbations optimized with a Lagrangian trust-region objective. Achieves up to 25% return improvement over baselines across manipulation, locomotion, and dexterous tasks while maintaining higher action-space entropy than unconstrained steering.
abstract: Behavior cloning with high-capacity generative policies achieves strong imitation performance, but is often limited by demonstration coverage and distribution shift. Direct reinforcement learning fine-tuning can improve performance, but updating large action decoders is frequently unstable and sample inefficient. We propose Lagrangian Perturbation Diffusion Steering (LP-DS), a lightweight adaptation method that improves a frozen generative policy by learning a compact noise-space perturbation before decoding. LP-DS optimizes this perturbation with a Lagrangian trust-region objective, improving downstream value while constraining deviation from the latent prior. Across RoboMimic manipulation, OpenAI Gym locomotion, and Adroit dexterous manipulation benchmarks, LP-DS improves sample efficiency, success, and return while maintaining higher action-space entropy than unconstrained noise-space steering, with return improvements of up to 25% over prior baselines. Additional evaluations with flow-matching backbones, a large vision-language-action model, and physical Franka deployment show that LP-DS is not limited to compact diffusion policies or simulated benchmarks.
notes: High — lightweight RL adaptation of frozen diffusion policies in latent noise space (ICML 2026)

title: Whole-Body Constrained Learning for Legged Locomotion via Hierarchical Optimization
authors: Haoyu Wang, Ruyi Zhou, Liang Ding, Tie Liu, Zhelin Zhang, Peng Xu, Haibo Gao, Zongquan Deng
headline: Hierarchical optimization adds hard safety constraints to RL locomotion on real hexapod
summary: Designs a hierarchical optimization-based whole-body follower integrating hard and soft constraints into the RL framework for legged locomotion. Deployed on a hexapod robot in outdoor environments including snow-covered slopes and stairs, demonstrating traversability and safety while mitigating sim-to-real transfer challenges.
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated impressive performance in legged locomotion over various challenging environments. However, due to the sim-to-real gap and lack of explainability, unconstrained RL policies deployed in the real world still suffer from inevitable safety issues, such as joint collisions, excessive torque, or foot slippage in low-friction environments. These problems limit its usage in missions with strict safety requirements, such as planetary exploration, nuclear facility inspection, and deep-sea operations. In this paper, we design a hierarchical optimization-based whole-body follower, which integrates both hard and soft constraints into RL framework to make the robot move with better safety guarantees. Leveraging the advantages of model-based control, our approach allows for the definition of various types of hard and soft constraints during training or deployment, which allows for policy fine-tuning and mitigates the challenges of sim-to-real transfer. Meanwhile, it preserves the robustness of RL when dealing with locomotion in complex unstructured environments. The trained policy with introduced constraints was deployed in a hexapod robot and tested in various outdoor environments, including snow-covered slopes and stairs, demonstrating the great traversability and safety of our approach.
notes: Moderate — hierarchical optimization for safe RL locomotion on real hardware; addresses sim-to-real safety

title: SafeVLA-Bench: A Benchmark for the Success-Safety Gap in Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Jialiang Fan, Weizhe Xu, Oleg Sokolsky, Insup Lee, Fanxin Kong
matched_interests: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs)|Adversarial robustness of robot policies|Signal Temporal Logic (STL)|Safety benchmarking for learned policies
theme_groups: Safety & Verification|VLA & Generalist Policies|Formal Methods & STL
headline: STL-based safety benchmark reveals 13-56% of successful VLA rollouts are unsafe
summary: Presents SafeVLA-Bench, a post-hoc safety framework formalizing task-aware safety requirements as STL specifications. Introduces Succ-But-Unsafe and Violation Severity Index metrics. Finds that 13-15% of successful tabletop rollouts and 36-56% of successful RoboCasa-365 rollouts violate at least one safety clause, exposing a significant success-safety gap.
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) benchmarks measure whether a policy completes a requested manipulation task, but binary success can hide safety-relevant trajectory behavior: reaching the goal while applying excessive contact, disturbing bystander objects, destabilizing the held object, or entering robot self-contact. We present SafeVLA-Bench, a post-hoc safety-evaluation framework for existing simulator-based VLA benchmarks. It formalizes task-aware safety requirements as Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications and reports native success with two unsafe-success metrics: Succ-But-Unsafe (SBU), the fraction of rollouts that both succeed and violate safety, and Violation Severity Index (VSI), a bounded worst-violation depth score. We instantiate SafeVLA-Bench on LIBERO and RoboCasa-365, evaluating nine policy-benchmark entries across tabletop and kitchen manipulation tasks. High task success does not imply safe execution: high-SR tabletop baselines still leave 13-15% unsafe-episode rates, and 36-56% of successful RoboCasa-365 rollouts violate at least one active safety clause.
notes: High — STL-based safety evaluation of VLA policies revealing success-safety gap in standard benchmarks

title: EgoSafetyBench: A Diagnostic Egocentric Video Benchmark for Evaluating Embodied VLMs as Runtime Safety Guards
authors: Siddhant Panpatil, Arth Singh, Mijin Koo, Chaeyun Kim, Haon Park, Dasol Choi
matched_interests: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs)|Runtime verification of learned policies|Adversarial robustness of robot policies
headline: Egocentric benchmark shows VLM safety guards miss contextual hazards and are degraded by misleading signs
summary: Introduces EgoSafetyBench with 1200 robot-view scenarios annotated at half-second granularity to evaluate VLMs as streaming safety guards. Finds that guards reliably detect hazards but miss specific hazardous moments, especially contextual ones. Misleading in-scene text degrades all tested guards, with vulnerable models missing up to a third of hazards.
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are now proposed as runtime safety guards for embodied agents in homes and factories. A deployable guard must catch genuinely unsafe situations while avoiding unnecessary intervention on routine but superficially alarming activity, a distinction that binary safety benchmarks obscure. We introduce EgoSafetyBench, an egocentric video benchmark of 1,200 robot-view scenarios annotated at half-second granularity, to evaluate VLMs as streaming guards across two tracks. The situational track (800 scenarios) spans four families, from routine and safe-but-suspicious scenes to obvious and contextual hazards. The visual-channel track (400 scenarios) targets in-scene text -- a sign, sticker, or label visible in the scene -- that can misrepresent the physical situation, pairing each misleading sign with a truthful version to test both whether a guard flags the text as misleading and whether the text corrupts its physical-safety judgment. Both tracks use contrastive ladders: near-identical scenarios differing only in a single visible deciding cue, so a correct call must hinge on that cue rather than the overall scene type. We evaluate ten open- and closed-source VLMs. We find that while guards reliably recognize videos containing hazards, they often miss specific hazardous moments, particularly contextual hazards. Furthermore, misleading in-scene signs degrade all tested guards: vulnerable models miss up to a third of hazards, while robust models over-intervene on safe content. Matched controls reveal that apparent safety robustness often reflects indiscriminate alarming rather than true physical reasoning.
notes: High — diagnostic benchmark for VLMs as runtime safety guards with contrastive egocentric scenarios

title: Improving Robotic Generalist Policies via Flow Reversal Steering
authors: Andy Tang, William Chen, Andrew Wagenmaker, Chelsea Finn, Sergey Levine
matched_interests: Flow matching|Generalist policies|Imitation learning|Inference-time policy steering
headline: Flow reversal steers generalist policies with semantic guidance for up to 95% success boost
summary: Proposes Flow Reversal Steering (FRS): takes suboptimal actions, finds their latent noises by passing through a flow policy in reverse, and maps them to nearby generalist action modes. Enables VLM-guided zero-shot control, behavioral cloning distillation with 95% absolute success boosts in under a minute, and RL bootstrapping with semantic knowledge.
abstract: Generalist policies can learn a wide range of skills from diverse robot datasets. In order to solve or improve on challenging new tasks, we need a way to infer and invoke the appropriate actions from the policy's rich behavioral prior, especially when directly commanding the policy fails. We focus on flow matching generalists and propose Flow Reversal Steering (FRS): a method that takes suboptimal but reasonable actions, finds their latent noises by passing them through the flow policy in reverse, and maps them to nearby generalist action modes. We evaluate FRS across many simulated and real-world manipulation settings. First, FRS can turn coarse semantic guidance from humans or vision-language models (VLMs) into corresponding good robot actions, improving zero-shot control. These gains can be distilled with behavioral cloning by training an auxiliary policy to output noises that the generalist maps to good actions -- showing up to 95% absolute task success rate boosts in under a minute of training. Finally, FRS enables policy improvement by bootstrapping reinforcement learning with semantic knowledge, improving on several tasks that standard RL fails to improve on.
notes: High — flow reversal method to steer generalist policies using semantic guidance with VLM integration

title: HazardArena: Evaluating Semantic Safety in Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Zixing Chen, Yifeng Gao, Li Wang, Yunhan Zhao, Yi Liu, Jiayu Li, Xiang Zheng, Zuxuan Wu, Cong Wang, Xingjun Ma, Yu-Gang Jiang
matched_interests: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs)|Adversarial robustness of robot policies|Safety benchmarking for learned policies
headline: Twin safe/unsafe scenarios expose VLA semantic safety failures and propose training-free mitigation
summary: Introduces HazardArena with 2000+ assets and 40 risk-sensitive tasks spanning 7 real-world risk categories. Uses safe/unsafe twin scenarios differing only in semantic context. Finds VLAs trained on safe scenarios fail in unsafe counterparts. Proposes a training-free Safety Option Layer using semantic attributes or a VL judge to reduce unsafe behaviors.
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models inherit rich world knowledge from vision-language backbones and acquire executable skills via action demonstrations. However, existing evaluations largely focus on action execution success, leaving action policies loosely coupled with visual-linguistic semantics. This decoupling exposes a systematic vulnerability whereby correct action execution may induce unsafe outcomes under semantic risk. To expose this vulnerability, we introduce HazardArena, a benchmark designed to evaluate semantic safety in VLAs under controlled yet risk-bearing contexts. HazardArena is constructed from safe/unsafe twin scenarios that share matched objects, layouts, and action requirements, differing only in the semantic context that determines whether an action is unsafe. We find that VLA models trained exclusively on safe scenarios often fail to behave safely when evaluated in their corresponding unsafe counterparts. HazardArena includes over 2,000 assets and 40 risk-sensitive tasks spanning 7 real-world risk categories grounded in established robotic safety standards. To mitigate this vulnerability, we propose a training-free Safety Option Layer that constrains action execution using semantic attributes or a vision-language judge, substantially reducing unsafe behaviors with minimal impact on task performance. We hope that HazardArena highlights the need to rethink how semantic safety is evaluated and enforced in VLAs as they scale toward real-world deployment.
notes: High — semantic safety benchmark for VLAs with twin safe/unsafe scenarios and training-free safety layer

title: IS-Bench: Evaluating Interactive Safety of VLM-Driven Embodied Agents in Daily Household Tasks
authors: Xiaoya Lu, Zeren Chen, Xuhao Hu, Yijin Zhou, Weichen Zhang, Dongrui Liu, Lu Sheng, Jing Shao
matched_interests: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs)|Runtime verification of learned policies|Safety benchmarking for learned policies
headline: First interactive safety benchmark reveals VLM agents lack dynamic risk awareness in household tasks
summary: Presents IS-Bench with 161 scenarios and 388 unique safety risks in a high-fidelity simulator. Proposes process-oriented evaluation verifying whether risk mitigation actions are performed in correct procedural order. Finds GPT-4o and Gemini-2.5 series agents lack interactive safety awareness; safety-aware CoT helps but compromises task completion.
abstract: Flawed planning from VLM-driven embodied agents poses significant safety hazards, hindering their deployment in real-world household tasks. However, existing static, non-interactive evaluation paradigms fail to adequately assess risks within these interactive environments, since they cannot simulate dynamic risks that emerge from an agent's actions and rely on unreliable post-hoc evaluations that ignore unsafe intermediate steps. To bridge this critical gap, we propose evaluating an agent's interactive safety: its ability to perceive emergent risks and execute mitigation steps in the correct procedural order. We thus present IS-Bench, the first multi-modal benchmark designed for interactive safety, featuring 161 challenging scenarios with 388 unique safety risks instantiated in a high-fidelity simulator. Crucially, it facilitates a novel process-oriented evaluation that verifies whether risk mitigation actions are performed before/after specific risk-prone steps. Extensive experiments on leading VLMs, including the GPT-4o and Gemini-2.5 series, reveal that current agents lack interactive safety awareness, and that while safety-aware Chain-of-Thought can improve performance, it often compromises task completion. By highlighting these critical limitations, IS-Bench provides a foundation for developing safer and more reliable embodied AI systems.
notes: Moderate — interactive safety benchmark for VLM household agents (AAAI 2026)

title: How Does the Lagrangian Guide Safe Reinforcement Learning through Diffusion Models?
authors: Xiaoyuan Cheng, Wenxuan Yuan, Boyang Li, Yuanchao Xu, Yiming Yang, Hao Liang, Bei Peng, Robert Loftin, Zhuo Sun, Yukun Hu
matched_interests: Diffusion models|Safe & robust robot control|Reinforcement learning
headline: Augmented Lagrangian stabilizes safe RL with diffusion policies by convexifying energy landscape
summary: Proposes ALGD for off-policy safe RL with diffusion policies. Shows the Lagrangian acts as an energy function guiding denoising dynamics, but direct usage destabilizes policy generation. Introduces an augmented Lagrangian that locally convexifies the energy landscape, yielding stable safe policy generation without altering the optimal policy distribution.
abstract: Diffusion policy sampling enables reinforcement learning (RL) to represent multimodal action distributions beyond suboptimal unimodal Gaussian policies. However, existing diffusion-based RL methods primarily focus on offline setting for reward maximization, with limited consideration of safety in online settings. To address this gap, we propose Augmented Lagrangian-Guided Diffusion (ALGD), a novel algorithm for off-policy safe RL. By revisiting optimization theory and energy-based modeling, we show that the instability of primal-dual methods arises from the nonconvex Lagrangian landscape. In diffusion-based safe RL, the Lagrangian can be interpreted as an energy function guiding the denoising dynamics; counter-intuitively, direct usage destabilizes both policy generation and training. ALGD resolves this issue by introducing an augmented Lagrangian that locally convexifies the energy landscape, yielding a stabilized policy generation and training, without altering the distribution of optimal policy. Theoretical analysis and extensive experiments demonstrate that ALGD is both theoretically grounded and empirically effective, achieving strong and stable performance across diverse environments.
notes: High — augmented Lagrangian for stable safe RL with diffusion policies (ICML 2026)

title: On the Limits of Sampling-Based Reachability: Geometry, Dynamics, and Sample Complexity
authors: J Liu, I Tabbara, H Sibai, E Mallada
headline: Geometry and dynamics fundamentally bound the sample complexity of sampling-based reachability
summary: Sampling-based reachability is an increasingly popular alternative to Hamilton-Jacobi methods that scale poorly with state dimension, offering finite-sample coverage guarantees. This paper analyzes how the geometry of the initial set, the system dynamics, and the sampling law jointly determine sample complexity and the probability mass left uncovered. The results characterize when sampling-based verification is efficient versus fundamentally hard, directly informing data-driven verification of black-box systems.
abstract: Reachability analysis is central to safety-critical control, robotics, and neural network verification, but classical computational methods, such as Hamilton-Jacobi reachability and set propagation, scale poorly with state dimension. Sampling-based methods have emerged as a promising alternative, often providing finite-sample guarantees that bound the probability-mass left uncovered. However, an explicit account of how the geometry of the initial set, the dynamics, and the sampling law affect the achievable guarantees has been lacking. This work studies the fundamental limits of sampling-based reachability, relating sample complexity to geometric and dynamical properties of the system.
notes: Alert: Herbert citation. Core — sampling-based reachability sample complexity, directly tied to data-driven verification of black-box systems.

title: pacSTL: PAC-Bounded Signal Temporal Logic from Data-Driven Reachability Analysis
authors: H Krasowski, E Dietrich, EC Gezer, R Skjetne, et al.
headline: PAC-bounded STL semantics derived directly from data-driven reachability, enabling real-time uncertain-signal verification
summary: Standard Signal Temporal Logic has deterministic semantics that cannot accommodate uncertainty, and existing probabilistic extensions are computationally costly. pacSTL derives PAC (probably approximately correct) bounds on STL satisfaction directly from data-driven reachability analysis, avoiding repeated trajectory sampling or redesign of atomic-proposition distributions. This yields real-time-capable, distribution-free guarantees on temporal-logic specifications — a direct fit for data-driven verification of uncertain systems.
abstract: Signal Temporal Logic (STL) is an expressive language for specifying behaviors of dynamical systems from continuous signals. However, a limitation of standard STL is its inherently deterministic semantics, which prevents it from accommodating uncertainty. Existing approaches to overcome this limitation are computationally costly and limit real-time capability, requiring repeated trajectory sampling or redesign of probability distributions over atomic propositions whenever the atomic predicates change. We introduce pacSTL, which equips STL with PAC-bounded semantics computed from data-driven reachability analysis, providing distribution-free guarantees on specification satisfaction while retaining real-time capability.
notes: Alert: Lindemann/Tomlin/Bansal. Core — data-driven reachability + STL + PAC guarantees, central to data-driven verification.

title: Robust Adaptive Backup Control Barrier Functions
authors: E Daş, DEJ van Wijk, TG Molnar, AD Ames, JW Burdick
matched_interests: Control Barrier Functions (CBFs)|Safe & robust robot control
headline: Backup CBFs made robust to parametric uncertainty in both drift and actuation dynamics
summary: Backup control barrier functions guarantee safety by forward-simulating a known backup controller, but assume accurate dynamics. This work introduces robust adaptive backup CBFs for nonlinear control-affine systems with parametric uncertainty in both the drift and actuation matrix. The method adapts online while preserving safety guarantees, extending backup CBFs toward realistic uncertain settings.
abstract: We propose a notion of robust adaptive backup control barrier functions for nonlinear control affine systems with parametric uncertainty in both the drift dynamics and actuation matrix. Backup control barrier functions guarantee safety by predicting the evolution of the system under a backup controller. We extend this framework to be robust to parametric uncertainty and to adapt online, providing safety guarantees despite model uncertainty.
notes: Alert: Lindemann/Herbert/Tomlin/Bansal. High — CBF theory (van Wijk/Ames group) for robust safe control under model uncertainty.

title: End-to-End Learning of Safe Optimal Feedback Control in High Dimensions with Control Barrier Function Layers
authors: X Li, K Kan, D Verma, K Kumar, S Osher, SW Fung
matched_interests: Control Barrier Functions (CBFs)|Safe & robust robot control
headline: Embedding differentiable CBF-QP layers to learn safe high-dimensional feedback controllers end-to-end
summary: Learning high-dimensional feedback controllers under hard safety constraints requires embedding a quadratic program (the CBF-QP) inside end-to-end training. This paper develops CBF layers that make this tractable in high dimensions, learning semi-global safe optimal feedback policies. It bridges learned control and formal CBF safety guarantees for high-dimensional systems.
abstract: We consider the problem of learning high-dimensional semi-global feedback controllers under hard safety constraints enforced by control barrier functions (CBFs). Incorporating CBFs into end-to-end policy training requires embedding a quadratic program in the computational graph, which is challenging to scale. We propose control barrier function layers that enable differentiable, scalable training of safe optimal feedback controllers in high dimensions, combining optimality objectives with formal safety guarantees.
notes: Alert: Herbert/Tomlin/Bansal. High — learning-based safe control with CBF layers, connects learned controllers to formal safety.

title: Robust reachability within deep reinforcement learning framework
authors: S Marthi, MS Jha, D Theilliol, JC Ponsart
matched_interests: Hamilton-Jacobi reachability|Reinforcement learning|Safe & robust robot control
headline: Solving Hamilton-Jacobi reachability as optimal control inside a DDPG actor-critic framework
summary: This work recasts Hamilton-Jacobi reachability for nonlinear control-affine systems with disturbances as an optimal control problem solved by deep RL. In a DDPG framework, the critic learns the HJ reachability value function while the actor synthesizes the optimal safe policy, aided by a Telescopic Incentive Reward Function for efficient learning. It offers a learning-based route to scalable robust reachability.
abstract: We propose a novel deep reinforcement learning based approach to solve Hamilton-Jacobi reachability (HJ-R) problem for nonlinear control-affine systems with external disturbance. By recasting reachability as an optimal control problem, we solve it within a Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) framework: the critic learns the HJ-R value function and the actor synthesizes the optimal policy. We propose a Telescopic Incentive Reward Function (TIRF) that makes the learning process efficient and improves convergence for robust reachability estimation.
notes: Alert: Herbert citation. High — learning-based HJ reachability, adjacent to data-driven verification and safe control.

title: GuidedAttention: Interpretable and Correctable Visual Attention for OOD-Robust Robot Manipulation via Imitation Learning
authors: M Murooka, R Nakajo, K Shirai, T Motoda, H Oh, et al.
matched_interests: Verification of visuomotor policies|Imitation learning|Diffusion models|Adversarial robustness of robot policies
headline: Interpretable, human-correctable attention keypoints make diffusion visuomotor policies OOD-robust
summary: End-to-end visuomotor policies offer humans little insight into or control over what the policy attends to. GuidedAttention predicts task-relevant attention keypoints from images as an explicit intermediate representation that conditions a diffusion action policy, and lets users inspect and correct keypoints at rollout. This improves out-of-distribution robustness while adding interpretability to learned manipulation — relevant to verifying visuomotor policies.
abstract: End-to-end visuomotor policies provide little opportunity for humans to understand or correct the policy's visual attention. We propose GuidedAttention, a visuomotor imitation learning framework that introduces interpretable and correctable visual attention as an explicit intermediate representation. Task-relevant attention keypoints are predicted from camera images and condition a diffusion-based action policy. Users can inspect and optionally correct selected keypoints once at rollout time, improving out-of-distribution robustness while providing interpretability into the policy's decision-making.
notes: Alert: Bajcsy citation. High — interpretable/correctable attention for diffusion visuomotor policies, relevant to verification of visuomotor policies.

title: Trust Your Instincts: Confidence-Driven Test-Time RL for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: S Chen, J Yuan, J Wang, T Chen
headline: Confidence signals drive test-time RL for VLAs without external environmental feedback
summary: RL is increasingly used to push VLAs beyond static imitation, but usually needs external environmental reward. This paper uses the model's own confidence as an intrinsic signal for confidence-driven test-time reinforcement learning, adapting VLA policies online without predefined feedback. It ties into inference-time steering and uncertainty-based adaptation of learned policies.
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become indispensable for pushing Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) beyond static imitation learning. However, existing RL methods typically require external environmental feedback, relying on predefined reward signals that are costly or unavailable at deployment. We propose a confidence-driven test-time RL approach that leverages the model's own confidence as an intrinsic reward, enabling VLAs to self-improve at test time without external supervision.
notes: Alert: Bajcsy related. High — test-time RL + confidence/uncertainty for VLAs, ties to inference-time steering and UQ threads.

title: When Internal Feedback Goodharts: SAE Rewards Fail to Improve Robot Success
authors: S Osorio, JZ Yang
headline: Negative result: sparse-autoencoder internal features are poor reward proxies for diffusion robot policies
summary: Sparse autoencoders expose interpretable internal features in diffusion robot policies, prompting hopes they could serve as dense reward proxies. In a controlled study on Octo-Base in SimplerEnv, the authors show these features Goodhart — they correlate with task structure but fail to improve robot success when used as rewards. The negative result cautions against using mechanistic-interpretability features as feedback signals.
abstract: World feedback for robot learning is sparse and delayed, motivating dense proxy signals for filtering, credit assignment, or fine-tuning. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) expose dense internal features in diffusion robot policies, but it is unclear whether such features are useful feedback or merely interpretable correlates. We report a controlled negative result testing this boundary in Octo-Base on SimplerEnv. SAE features show task and phase structure, native-state local action selectivity, and other interpretable properties, yet using them as rewards fails to improve robot success, indicating a Goodhart-style gap between interpretability and useful feedback.
notes: Alert: Tomlin citation. Moderate — mechanistic interpretability (SAEs) of diffusion policies; negative result relevant to verifying visuomotor policies.

title: Learning Personalized Safety Interventions for Haptic Human-Robot Shared Control
authors: D Zhang, R Tron
headline: Learning user-preferred haptic safety interventions from sparse demonstrations for shared control
summary: Haptic guidance systems typically use fixed intervention strategies that ignore individual users' safety preferences. This Learning-from-Haptics framework learns personalized safety interventions from sparse demonstrations, adapting shared-control behavior to each user. It combines imitation learning with safety-preference modeling for human-robot shared control.
abstract: Haptic feedback provides an implicit channel for communicating safety intentions during human-robot shared control. Existing haptic guidance systems typically employ predefined intervention strategies that cannot accommodate the diverse safety preferences of individual users or application scenarios. To address this limitation, we propose a Learning from Haptics (LfH) framework that learns user-preferred safety interventions from sparse demonstrations, eliminating the need for hand-tuned intervention rules and adapting shared-control assistance to individual users.
notes: Alert: Herbert/Lindemann citation. Moderate — learning safety interventions from demonstrations, adjacent to safe control and imitation learning.

title: Performant robotic manipulation with real-world reinforcement learning
authors: K Lei, H Li, D Yu, Z Wei, L Guo, Z Jiang, Z Wang, et al.
headline: RL-100 unifies imitation and RL in the diffusion denoising process for reliable real-world manipulation
summary: RL-100 is a real-world RL framework built on diffusion visuomotor policies that targets human-level reliability in manipulation. It unifies imitation and reinforcement learning under a single clipped-PPO surrogate objective applied within the diffusion denoising process. Published in Science Robotics, it demonstrates high task success under a rigorous real-world evaluation protocol.
abstract: Real-world robotic manipulation in homes and factories demands reliability, efficiency, and robustness that approach or surpass skilled human operators. We present a real-world reinforcement learning (RL) framework, RL-100, for achieving complete task success under a predefined evaluation protocol built on diffusion visuomotor policies. RL-100 unifies imitation and RL under a single clipped proximal policy optimization surrogate objective applied in the denoising process, yielding stable and efficient improvement of diffusion policies directly in the real world.
notes: Alert: Majumdar/Bajcsy related. High — Science Robotics; RL fine-tuning of diffusion visuomotor policies, core diffusion+RL intersection.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning under Regularized Probabilistic Counterexample Guidance
authors: X Ji, A Filieri
venue: ACM Transactions on Autonomous and Adaptive Systems
headline: Counterexample-guided safe RL that regularizes exploration under sparse or incomplete knowledge
summary: Safe exploration is a core obstacle for RL in safety-critical systems, and existing approaches degrade when model knowledge is sparse or incomplete. This paper introduces a counterexample-guided RL method that uses regularized probabilistic counterexamples to steer exploration away from unsafe behaviors. It connects formal-methods-style counterexample generation with safe reinforcement learning.
abstract: Safe exploration in reinforcement learning remains a critical challenge for safety-critical autonomous systems, where the typical trial-and-error learning process can lead to hazardous outcomes. While several existing approaches incorporate kinematic models or external knowledge to limit the exploration of unsafe behaviors, their effectiveness is significantly weakened in the presence of incomplete or sparse knowledge. This paper introduces a counterexample-guided reinforcement learning approach that uses regularized probabilistic counterexamples to guide safe policy learning, improving safety during exploration without requiring complete model knowledge.
notes: Alert: Majumdar citation. Moderate — counterexample-guided safe RL, bridges formal verification ideas and reinforcement learning.

title: Robustness of Robotic Manipulation: Foundations and Frontiers
authors: Y Dong, Z Sun, L Yang, M Baum, K Ikemura, S Song, et al.
matched_interests: Adversarial robustness of robot policies|Safe & robust robot control
headline: A unifying survey of robustness in robotic manipulation: foundations, taxonomy, and open frontiers
summary: Robots remain far behind humans in robust physical manipulation, partly for lack of a unified conceptual framework. This survey organizes the fragmented literature on manipulation robustness into common foundations and identifies open research frontiers. It is a broad reference rather than a new method, useful for situating robustness/verification work.
abstract: Humans and animals exhibit remarkable robustness in physical manipulation, yet robots remain far behind. Progress toward human-level manipulation robustness is hindered by the absence of a unified and systematic understanding: different communities study robustness under different assumptions, metrics, and threat models. This survey consolidates the foundations of robotic manipulation robustness, proposes a taxonomy spanning perturbation types and evaluation protocols, and outlines open frontiers toward reliable, robust manipulation.
notes: Alert: Bajcsy related. Moderate — robustness survey for manipulation [residual -1: survey, no new method or data-driven verification contribution].

title: DWM: Separating World Effects from Actions in Latent World Models
authors: YG Zhang, T Du, Q Zhang, Y Wang
headline: Disentangling action effects from world dynamics improves latent world-model transition learning
summary: Action-conditioned latent world models supervise the next-latent transition with a single undifferentiated target, forcing one signal to absorb both action effects and autonomous world dynamics. DWM separates world effects from action effects in the latent transition, giving a cleaner, more structured learning signal. This improves model-based control built on latent world models.
abstract: Latent world models underpin much of modern model-based control, yet current action-conditioned formulations supervise the next-latent transition with a single, undifferentiated target, forcing a monolithic learning signal to absorb every source of change. We propose DWM, which explicitly separates world effects from action effects in latent world models, disentangling autonomous dynamics from action-induced changes to yield more structured and accurate predictive transitions for planning and control.
notes: Alert: Bajcsy related. High — latent world models for model-based control, matches the world-models-for-robotics interest.

title: SAGE: Subgoal-Conditioned Action Generation for Latent World Model Planning
authors: L Cheng, Q Zhang, Y Wang
matched_interests: World models for robotics|Sampling-based motion planning
headline: Subgoal-conditioned action generation makes latent world-model planning scale over long horizons
summary: Latent world models plan by imagining and evaluating candidate action sequences with a learned internal simulator, but planning quality degrades as horizons grow. SAGE introduces subgoal-conditioned action generation to structure long-horizon planning within latent world models. This improves the reach and reliability of world-model-based planning.
abstract: Latent world models have emerged as a powerful planning paradigm by learning action-conditioned predictive dynamics and using them as internal simulators to imagine and evaluate candidate action sequences. However, as the planning horizon grows, action search becomes inefficient and predictions drift. We propose SAGE, a subgoal-conditioned action generation method that structures planning within latent world models, improving long-horizon performance and sample efficiency.
notes: Alert: Bajcsy related. High — latent world-model planning, matches world-models-for-robotics and planning interests.

title: 3D Point World Models: Point Completion Enables More Accurate Dynamics Learning
authors: S Peri, H Nguyen, C Kim, L Fuxin, S Lee
headline: Adding explicit 3D point structure and completion sharpens world-model dynamics prediction
summary: Large video-based dynamics models lack explicit 3D spatial structure and predict poorly for control. This work builds world models over 3D point representations and shows that point completion improves the accuracy of learned dynamics. Explicit 3D structure yields more reliable predictive models for robotic planning.
abstract: Learning predictive models of the world enables robotic control through planning, potentially allowing robots to improvise solutions on new tasks. However, large video-based dynamics models lack explicit 3D spatial structure and suffer from geometric inconsistency, degrading control performance. We introduce 3D Point World Models, which operate over point-cloud representations and use point completion to fill occluded structure, enabling more accurate dynamics learning and improved planning.
notes: Alert: Majumdar related. High — 3D-structured world models for dynamics/planning, matches world-models-for-robotics interest.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Flow-Matching Policies with Density Transport
authors: Boshu Lei, Kostas Daniilidis, Antonio Loquercio
headline: Online RL fine-tunes flow-matching policies by transporting action densities toward high reward
summary: RLDT views RL-based policy improvement as density transport aligned with flow matching's formulation, using Stein Variational Gradient Descent to construct transport fields from a maximum-entropy RL objective. The method fine-tunes pretrained flow-matching policies via expected-target estimation from intermediate denoising steps, avoiding unstable backpropagation through time. Experiments show RLDT outperforms baselines across dense/sparse reward tasks and vision-based robot manipulation.
abstract: We present an online reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm for fine-tuning flow-matching policies in continuous-control problems. Our key insight is to view RL-based policy improvement as a transport of action densities towards regions of high reward, which naturally aligns with the transport formulation of flow matching models. Prior methods either approximate the current or optimal policy distribution or resort to distillation, which introduces biased gradients or sacrifices multimodal modeling capacity. In contrast, our approach for RL with Density Transport, which we name RLDT, constructs a transport field from a maximum-entropy RL objective using Stein Variational Gradient Descent (SVGD). Then, it finetunes a pretrained flow matching policy to align with this field. Training with this alignment objective is nontrivial because flow-matching policies generate actions via a multi-step process, making direct gradient-based optimization challenging. To overcome this challenge and stabilize training, we approximate policy actions from intermediate denoising steps via expected-target estimation. This allows the transport-field update to propagate into the network parameters without unstable backpropagation through time. Experimental results demonstrate that RLDT outperforms competitive baselines in reward quality and convergence speed. This performance holds across diverse continuous-control tasks, encompassing both dense and sparse rewards, as well as state- and vision-based long-horizon robot manipulation.
notes: High — flow matching + RL for robot control; connects generative policy models to reward-driven improvement

title: Semantically Structured Mixture-of-Experts for Compositional Robotic Manipulation
authors: Chengyu Deng, Guanqi Chen, Yizhou Chen, Zejia Liu, Zhiwen Ruan, Guanhua Chen, Jia Pan
headline: VLM-supervised semantic routing gives MoE diffusion policies interpretable skill decomposition and compositional transfer
summary: Introduces SMoDP, which grounds MoE expert specialization in semantic task structure by using VLM-supervised skill predictors to route action chunks to behaviorally specialized experts. A dual contrastive alignment strategy grounds multi-modal observations in language-defined skill semantics while enforcing routing consistency. Outperforms diffusion and MoE baselines on multi-task benchmarks with improved parameter efficiency and compositional transfer.
abstract: Diffusion-based policies have established a new standard for precise robotic manipulation but face a critical scalability bottleneck: high-performance models are computationally expensive, while lightweight alternatives often fail to generalize across diverse multi-task environments. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures offer a promising path to efficiency by activating only a subset of parameters. However, existing MoE routing mechanisms typically rely on low-level noise or latent statistics, ignoring the compositional nature of manipulation tasks. This can fragment reusable behaviors across experts, limiting interpretability and transferability. We introduce Semantically Structured Mixture-of-Experts Diffusion Policy (SMoDP) for compositional robotic manipulation, a framework that grounds expert specialization in semantic task structure. SMoDP leverages a lightweight, inference-time skill predictor, supervised by offline annotations from Vision-Language Models (VLMs), to route action chunks to experts specialized for specific behavioral phases. To ensure robust assignment, we propose a dual contrastive alignment strategy that grounds multi-modal observations in language-defined skill semantics (Inter-modal) while enforcing routing consistency across visually distinct but functionally related behaviors (Intra-modal). Our approach outperforms representative diffusion and MoE-based baselines on multi-task benchmarks with significantly improved parameter efficiency and demonstrates effective compositional transfer to novel tasks through parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
notes: High — MoE diffusion policy with semantic skill routing; compositional manipulation with interpretability angle

title: BayesFP: Posterior Estimation for Flow-Based Policies via Feynman-Kac Sampling
authors: Sreevardhan Sirigiri, Weiming Zhi, Fabio Ramos
matched_interests: Diffusion models|Flow matching|Safe & robust robot control
headline: Inference-time Bayesian sampling steers pretrained diffusion and flow policies toward safety constraints without retraining
summary: Formulates constrained trajectory generation for pretrained diffusion and flow-matching policies as Bayesian posterior sampling, extending the Feynman-Kac corrector framework to deterministic flow-matching policies. The method steers pre-trained policies toward feasible, safety-constrained trajectories at inference time without any retraining. Validated on Diffusion Policy, GR00T-N1.6, and pi0.5 checkpoints across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks.
abstract: Robots must generate trajectories that remain faithful to learned expert behavior while satisfying safety constraints and task-specific objectives specified only at inference time. We formulate constrained trajectory generation for pretrained diffusion and flow-matching policies as Bayesian posterior sampling, with the learned demonstration distribution as a prior and an inference-time, cost-derived likelihood tilting it toward feasible, optimal trajectories. To sample from this posterior without any retraining of the base policy, we leverage the Feynman-Kac corrector framework, originally formulated for diffusion models, and extend it to deterministic flow-matching policies. The result is a unified, inference-time, retraining-free sampler for diffusion and flow policies. We validate the approach on pretrained Diffusion Policy, GR00T-N1.6, and pi0.5 checkpoints across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, including planning around non-convex obstacles introduced at inference time, and show improvements over the base pi0.5 on zero-shot tasks.
notes: High — inference-time safety steering of pretrained flow/diffusion policies; connects to verification via constraint satisfaction

title: Teaming Linear Temporal Logic: Coordinated Behavior Specification in Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Thomas Fawcett, George Konidaris
headline: TeamingLTL extends LTL to specify cooperative behaviors in large partially-observable multi-agent systems
summary: Extends Linear Temporal Logic into TeamingLTL for specifying complex cooperative behaviors in large multi-agent systems with partial observability. Users specify behaviors or goals while deferring realization to automated task planning and allocation. Demonstrates use in program verification and creation of correct-by-design controllers for heterogeneous multi-agent systems.
abstract: Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) is a formal language that can be used to specify robot behaviors and goal states. We extend LTL to enable the specification of complex cooperative behaviors in a large multi-agent system (MAS). The extended language, TeamingLTL, models features commonly present in MAS such as partial observability and cooperation between agents. This enables a user to specify behaviors or goals while deferring the realization of those states to a separate, automated task planning and allocation system. We show how to specify the behavior of a MAS using TeamingLTL and use this formulation in program verification and the creation of correct-by-design controllers.
notes: Low — extends LTL for multi-agent systems; tangential to core verification interests but relevant to formal methods

title: To Do or Not to Do: Ensuring the Safety of Visuomotor Policies Learned from Demonstrations
authors: Riad Ahmed, Moniruzzaman Akash, Momotaz Begum
matched_interests: Verification of visuomotor policies|Safe & robust robot control|Imitation learning
headline: Policy-agnostic execution guarantee decides when visuomotor IL policies can safely act using set invariance theory
summary: Proposes 'execution guarantee,' a policy-agnostic safety measure that guarantees maximum task success for visuomotor imitation learning policies under minor runtime perturbations. Leverages view synthesis to identify safe state-space regions and Nagumo's sub-tangentiality condition for set invariance to prove and operationalize the safety guarantee. Validated on a Franka robot in simulation and real world across multiple IL policies.
abstract: Task success has historically been the primary measure of policy performance in imitation learning (IL) research. This characteristic strictly limits the ubiquitous applications of IL algorithms in field robotics where safety assurance, in addition to task-success, is of paramount importance. It is often desirable for an IL-powered robot in the field not to roll out a policy, and hence score a poor performance, if the safety is not guaranteed. Although this trade-off between safety and performance is well investigated in classical control literature, policy safety is a heavily underexplored domain in IL research. The paper proposes execution guarantee, a policy-agnostic safety measure that guarantees the maximum task success for a visuomotor IL policy, despite minor run-time changes, from within a specific region in the state space, leveraging recent advances in view synthesis to identify such regions and exploring Nagumo's sub-tangentiality condition to prove and operationalize execution guarantee. Experiments with a Franka robot, both in simulation and real world, demonstrate how the proposed safety analysis allows various IL policies to achieve maximum task success with guarantee.
notes: Core — safety guarantees for visuomotor IL policies using set invariance; directly addresses verification of learned visuomotor controllers [residual +1: directly addresses safety verification of visuomotor policies, Sumanth's next research direction]

title: Cost-Aware Adaptive Conformal Inference for Runtime Assurance in Dynamic Environments
authors: Taoran Wu, Jingduo Pan, Luke Ong, Bai Xue
headline: Cost-aware conformal inference adapts uncertainty margins by violation severity for runtime safety in dynamic environments
summary: Proposes Cost-Aware Adaptive Conformal Inference (ACI) that incorporates constraint violation costs into the conformal adaptation mechanism, providing dual statistical guarantees bounding both violation frequencies and cumulative violation cost. By weighting prediction failures according to severity, the controller responds proportionally while maintaining efficiency during nominal operation. Integrated into a robust control synthesis framework without requiring explicit model knowledge.
abstract: This paper addresses the problem of providing runtime assurance for systems operating online under unknown and potentially time-varying data distributions. We propose Cost-Aware Adaptive Conformal Inference (ACI), a novel framework that incorporates constraint violation costs directly into the conformal adaptation mechanism. Our key insight is that uncertainty margins should adapt not only to the frequency of constraint violations but also to their severity. We formalize this through a cost-aware loss function that couples the miscoverage indicator with violation costs. Unlike existing methods that regulate a single controlled metric, our approach provides a dual statistical guarantee: simultaneously bounding the long-run average violation frequencies (reliability) and cumulative violation cost (harm). By weighting prediction failures according to their severity, the algorithm enables the controller to respond proportionally to violation severity, expanding prediction sets aggressively when necessary while maintaining efficiency during nominal operation. We integrate Cost-Aware ACI into a robust control synthesis framework, creating a closed-loop system that balances task performance with runtime risk control without requiring explicit model knowledge. Experiments validate its effectiveness for online risk-aware controller synthesis.
notes: High — conformal prediction for runtime assurance with cost-aware adaptation; extends CP methods for safety-critical control

title: Formal Verification of Learned Multi-Agent Communication Policies via Decision Tree Distillation
authors: Ahmad Farooq, Kamran Iqbal
headline: Neural multi-agent policies distilled into decision trees enable formal verification with PCTL properties
summary: Presents the first end-to-end framework for safety verification of learned multi-agent communication policies through decision tree distillation. Neural policies are distilled into interpretable decision trees (97.9% fidelity), translated to PRISM model checker specifications, and compositionally verified against 18 temporal logic properties. Monte Carlo validation confirms verified safety properties transfer to original neural policies with <0.6pp deviation.
abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables autonomous agents to develop sophisticated coordination strategies through emergent communication, but the resulting neural network policies lack the formal safety guarantees required for deployment in safety-critical robotic applications such as drone swarms and autonomous vehicle fleets. We present the first end-to-end framework for safety verification of learned multi-agent communication policies through policy abstraction: neural policies are distilled into interpretable decision trees, which are then formally verified, with empirical validation confirming that verified safety properties transfer to the original networks. Our four-stage pipeline consists of: (1) domain-specific feature extraction from agent observations, (2) decision tree distillation achieving 97.9% +/- 1.2% fidelity to neural network policies, (3) automated translation to PRISM probabilistic model checker specifications with complete feature-to-state-variable correspondence, and (4) compositional verification of Probabilistic Computation Tree Logic (PCTL) properties via pairwise decomposition with union-bound aggregation and empirical neighbor modeling. Evaluating Vector-Quantized Variational Information Bottleneck (VQ-VIB) policies for multi-drone coordination with 5-7 agents, we verify 18 temporal logic properties across safety, liveness, and cooperation categories, achieving 88.9% property satisfaction with all five safety thresholds satisfied (0.3% collision probability vs. 1% threshold). Monte Carlo validation of the original neural policies confirms that verified safety properties transfer with <0.6 percentage-point deviation (95% CI). Discrete VQ-VIB messages provide +11.6 to +13.6 percentage point fidelity advantages over continuous communication methods, enabling 3-4x faster verification. Our framework provides empirically validated safety verification for distilled policy abstractions, which serves as a practical bridge between deep MARL and the formal safety workflows required for multi-robot deployment.
notes: High — formal verification of learned policies via decision tree distillation; directly relevant to data-driven verification of black-box controllers

title: SCP-NL2TL: Selective Conformal Prediction with Semantic Verification for Natural Language to Temporal Logic Specifications
authors: Yixuan Wang, Licheng Luo, Yu Fu, Kaidi Xu, Yue Dong, Mingyu Cai
headline: Conformal risk control decides when LLM-generated temporal logic specs can be trusted for robot execution
summary: Proposes a selective translation framework for NL-to-temporal-logic that determines when generated specs can be trusted, using conformal risk control to calibrate accept/abstain decisions with distribution-free bounds. Combines back-translation fidelity and semantic equivalence dispersion as reliability signals, with a conformal anomaly detector screening OOD inputs. Validated across STL, LTL, and Spatio-Temporal Logic specifications.
abstract: Translating natural language instructions into machine-interpretable formal specifications enables robots and autonomous systems to plan, reason, and formally verify their behavior. However, existing translation models typically generate a specification for every input, even when the result is unreliable or fails to capture the user's intent, creating risks in safety-critical applications. Inspired by selective conformal prediction, we propose a selective translation framework that not only generates formal specifications but also determines when they can be trusted. Reliability is scored by two complementary black-box signals, the fidelity of the specification back-translated into natural language and the dispersion of repeated translations under exact semantic equivalence, which fail on different errors and jointly separate incorrect translations more sharply than either alone. Conformal risk control calibrates this score into a decision that accepts a specification or abstains, with a distribution-free bound on the rate at which incorrect specifications are accepted for execution, and a conformal anomaly detector on instruction embeddings screens out-of-distribution inputs before any translation is attempted. The proposed framework is general across formal specification languages, with experiments on Signal Temporal Logic (STL), Linear Temporal Logic (LTL), and geometric Spatio-Temporal Logic (SpaTiaL) demonstrating improved translation reliability, robustness under the evaluated cross-tier shifts, and effective uncertainty-aware abstention. This work establishes a foundation for trustworthy natural language interfaces by enabling AI systems to recognize when generated specifications may not be reliable.
notes: High — conformal prediction ensures trustworthy NL-to-temporal-logic translation; connects CP with STL/LTL for safe robot task specification

title: Probabilistic Reachable-Action Verification of Visuomotor Policies via Set-Based Training
authors: Yanliang Huang, Zhuocheng Zhang, Peng Xie, Zhen Zhang, Wenyuan Wu, Majid Khadiv, Zhuoqi Zeng, Amr Alanwar
matched_interests: Verification of visuomotor policies|Data-driven verification|Latent-space safety analysis
headline: Freeze the vision encoder, verify the rest: certified action-reachability radii for visuomotor policies
summary: End-to-end reachability analysis of visuomotor policies is intractable because large visual encoders make set propagation expensive and hopelessly conservative. The authors freeze the encoder and confine zonotope propagation to a low-dimensional interface between encoder and policy, calibrating the interface set from held-out camera-pose perturbations. Set-based training then directly minimizes the terminal output-enclosure width, and rollout-level split conformal calibration converts action-deviation scores into a probabilistic reachable-action radius with finite-sample coverage. In manipulation experiments the radius shrinks without hurting closed-loop task capability, and behavior-only, observational-consistency, and pointwise-adversarial controls all leave a larger radius.
abstract: Reachability analysis for visuomotor policies is difficult because large visual encoders make end-to-end set propagation computationally expensive and excessively conservative. We therefore freeze the visual encoder and confine set propagation to a low-dimensional interface between it and the downstream policy, with the interface set calibrated from held-out camera-pose perturbations. Propagating this set through the policy with zonotopes yields a terminal output-enclosure width that set-based training optimizes directly. During evaluation, camera-pose perturbations are sampled from the prescribed distribution, and rollout-level split conformal calibration converts the resulting action-deviation scores into a probabilistic reachable-action radius with finite-sample coverage. In controlled manipulation experiments, set-based training reduces this radius while preserving closed-loop task capability, and matched behavior-only, observational-consistency, and pointwise-adversarial controls all leave a larger radius.
notes: Alert: Bajcsy citation. Core - freezes the visual encoder and verifies the low-dimensional policy interface with zonotopes plus conformal calibration [residual +1: directly addresses reachability verification of black-box visuomotor policies, Sumanth's exact focus]

title: Data-Driven Formal Methods for Complex Dynamical Systems: A Survey
authors: Behrad Samari, Alessandro Abate, Antoine Girard, Majid Zamani, Amy Nejati, Abolfazl Lavaei
headline: The field map for data-driven verification without models, organized across three methodological pillars
summary: Hundreds of papers now claim formal verification or synthesis guarantees from data alone, but the literature is scattered and hard to navigate. This survey organizes it around three pillars: (in)finite-abstraction techniques, functional certificates such as control barrier certificates, and compositional methods. Within each, guarantees are classified as statistical (PAC and scenario-based), Lipschitz-continuity-derived, or structure-exploiting. Deterministic systems get the bulk of the coverage, but the authors devote specific attention to the stochastic case and the distinct challenges it raises.
abstract: Data-driven approaches with formal guarantees have recently emerged as a powerful means for the verification and controller synthesis of complex dynamical systems. Interest in these methods is rapidly growing, as system models are often unavailable in practice, and challenges such as nonlinear behavior, uncertainty, and the curse of dimensionality typically render accurate modeling infeasible. These difficulties motivate leveraging limited data collected from the system while still providing formal guarantees on its overall behavior. The community has therefore proposed a few hundred articles on the development of data-driven frameworks that enable the formal verification and synthesis of dynamical systems without explicit models, addressing complex specifications beyond stability. Despite this rapid growth, existing results remain scattered and lack a coherent organization, limiting a clear understanding of their principles, distinctions, and practical potential. This survey fills this gap by providing a comprehensive overview of these data-driven methods for both deterministic and stochastic dynamical systems. We structure the literature around three main methodological pillars in formal methods: (in)finite-abstraction-based techniques, functional certificate approaches, such as control barrier certificates, and compositional methods. For each of these approaches, we classify the resulting data-driven guarantees into three main categories: (i) statistical guarantees grounded in probably approximately correct and scenario-based frameworks, (ii) guarantees derived from Lipschitz continuity, and (iii) guarantees exploiting structural properties. While the literature on deterministic systems is considerably richer, we also devote particular attention to the stochastic counterpart, highlighting the inherent differences and challenges that arise compared to the deterministic case.
notes: Alert: Lindemann/Tomlin/Fan/Herbert citation. Core - comprehensive map of the data-driven verification field, organized by abstraction, certificates, and compositional methods

title: Towards General Language-Conditioned Latent Safety Filters
authors: Ihab Tabbara, Yuxuan Yang, Hussein Sibai
matched_interests: Latent-space safety analysis|Safe & robust robot control|Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs)|Hamilton-Jacobi reachability
headline: Safety filters that take their constraints in natural language, not code
summary: Existing safety filters are constraint-specific and must be redesigned whenever the safety requirement changes, which does not scale to VLA policies that already accept arbitrary language tasks. The authors condition a Hamilton-Jacobi safety actor and critic on language-specified constraints so a single filter covers a family of requirements. They evaluate on pick-and-place, table-wiping, and block-stacking in the vision-based setting. Constraint violations drop, and the filters show partial transfer to unseen constraint instances within the evaluated families.
abstract: Robot policies are becoming increasingly general, with vision-language-action (VLA) models enabling a single policy to execute diverse tasks specified in natural language. Safe deployment, however, requires adapting not only to new tasks but also to varying safety requirements across users, environments, and applications. Existing safety filters remain largely constraint-specific and thus must be redesigned or relearned when safety requirements change. In this paper, we investigate language-conditioned safety filtering, in which a Hamilton-Jacobi safety actor and critic are conditioned on language-specified constraints. We evaluate this formulation across pick-and-place, table-wiping, and block-stacking tasks in the vision-based setting, examining its ability to enforce language-specified constraints and transfer to unseen constraint instances within the evaluated constraint families. Our experiments provide evidence that language-conditioned safety filters reduce constraint violations and exhibit partial transfer to unseen constraint instances.
notes: Alert: Bansal/Fan/Herbert/Tomlin/Bajcsy citation. Core - HJ safety actor-critic conditioned on natural-language constraints for VLA policies

title: Embodied AI Needs Interpretability
authors: S Joseph, Andrea Bajcsy, J Ferrando, C Last, T MacMillan
matched_interests: Mechanistic interpretability for VLAs|Verification of visuomotor policies
headline: End-to-end evaluation cannot certify that an embodied model learned the right thing
summary: A position piece arguing that interpretability is a prerequisite, not a nicety, for embodied AI. Robotics, UAVs, and autonomous vehicles act in open-ended physical environments where actions are irreversible, sensors are partial, and failures cause real harm. Under those conditions, end-to-end benchmark performance cannot establish that a model has learned the intended behavior rather than a correlated shortcut. Full text was not retrievable at digest time; metadata is provisional.
notes: Alert: Bajcsy new articles. Core - argues end-to-end evaluation cannot certify that an embodied model learned the right thing. NOTE: OpenReview is CAPTCHA-gated; abstract could not be retrieved and author list is from the Scholar alert, treat as provisional

title: CheckVLA: Execution-Time Verification with Action-Conditioned World Model for Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation
authors: Yushan Liu, Peibo Sun, Xintao Chao, Zhenyang Yang, Yifan Xie, Lingfeng Zhang, Shoujie Li, Chenyu Tang, Fang Chen, Xiao-Ping Zhang, Wenbo Ding
matched_interests: World models for robotics|Verification of visuomotor policies|Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs)
headline: Conformally calibrated runtime monitor catches VLA action chunks going wrong mid-execution
summary: VLA policies dispatch open-loop action chunks, so a deviation occurring after dispatch cannot be caught by commit-time confidence, and observation-only anomaly scores have no action-conditioned reference. CheckVLA verifies execution against a separately trained frozen action-conditioned world model, with a conformally calibrated risk threshold bounding the episode-level probability of an unnecessary first intervention. Latency-aware hard prefixing restricts replacement to still-deployable actions, and a keyframe bank preserves evidence of prior progress. On RoboCasa365 it reaches 36.1% average success against 27.6% for periodic replanning, and at a matched 5% false-alarm target action conditioning raises timely recall to 77.9% versus 48.6% observation-only.
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies commonly execute long-horizon mobile manipulation through open-loop action chunks, issuing multiple actions without receiving new high-level visual input. A committed chunk therefore implies how observations should evolve, but accidental deviations can violate this expectation while the remaining actions continue to propagate the error: commit-time policy confidence cannot react to a deviation that occurs after dispatch, and observation-only anomaly scores lack an action-conditioned reference for separating expected effects from unexplained changes. We propose CheckVLA, which verifies execution with a separately trained, frozen action-conditioned world model. A conformally calibrated risk threshold bounds the episode-level probability of an unnecessary first intervention and determines when to intervene, its exceedance controls how strongly the rewritten suffix retains the superseded chunk, latency-aware hard prefixing restricts replacement to actions that remain deployable, and an event-driven keyframe bank preserves evidence of prior progress across repairs. On RoboCasa365, under a common training recipe and a matched invocation budget, CheckVLA attains a 36.1% average success rate against 27.6% for periodic replanning (+8.5 points). At a matched 5% episode-level false-alarm target, action conditioning raises timely recall to 77.9%, against 48.6% for an observation-only control and 37.9% for an action-shuffled control. These simulation results support action-conditioned verification as a way to restore feedback during chunked execution while keeping the repair consistent with inference latency.
notes: Alert: Bajcsy. Core - conformally calibrated runtime verification of open-loop VLA action chunks using a frozen world model

title: Certifying Plans under Model Mismatch: A Trilemma for Reachability from Scarce Data
authors: Yanliang Huang, Zhen Zhang, Ahmad Hafez, Wenyuan Wu, Peng Xie, Zhuoqi Zeng, Amr Alanwar
headline: An impossibility result for certifying learned action chunks from a handful of real transitions
summary: When a sim-to-real policy is certified against target-system data consisting of only a few isolated one-step transitions, any deterministic certifier that is sound for all consistent target systems must either decline to certify or return an arbitrarily wide reachable tube. The authors formalize this as a trilemma among uniform trajectory containment, finite projected width, and unrestricted model-error behavior off-data, and derive a finite plan-dependent width lower bound for bounded smooth error classes. Their method ForeReach requires a declared componentwise Lipschitz bound, builds a set-membership envelope for the model error, propagates a zonotopic tube, and certifies only when every slice avoids the unsafe set. On two benchmarks calibration baselines stay narrow while losing containment off-support, whereas ForeReach declines on unsupported sequences.
abstract: Sim-to-real policies are designed under nominal dynamics, but target-system trials may yield only a few isolated one-step transitions. We study pre-execution certification of a fixed control sequence, such as an action chunk produced by a learned policy. If the sequence reaches an unobserved state-input region, the observations remain consistent with target systems whose trajectories separate along it by an arbitrarily large amount. Any deterministic certifier sound for all of them must then decline to certify or return a reachable tube with arbitrarily large projected width. For bounded smooth classes of the target-nominal model error, we derive a finite plan-dependent projected-width lower bound. These results expose a trilemma among uniform trajectory containment, finite projected width, and unrestricted model-error behavior beyond the observations. ForeReach requires a supplied componentwise Lipschitz bound on the model error. Observed transition pairs can refute this declaration but cannot establish it outside the observed locations. Conditional on a valid declaration, our method constructs a set-membership envelope for the model error, propagates a zonotopic reachable tube, and certifies only when propagation remains within the certification domain and every projected tube slice avoids the unsafe set. In two benchmark systems, calibration baselines may remain narrow after losing trajectory containment outside data support, whereas our method declines to certify unsupported sequences and recovers certification when relevant target data and sufficient obstacle clearance are available.
notes: Alert: Lindemann citation. Core - impossibility result plus a method for pre-execution certification of learned action chunks from a handful of transitions

title: Agentic Harnesses: LLM-Driven Verification Layers for Robot Autonomy
authors: Rohan Bhagra, Mahantesh Halapannavar, Uddhav Bhattarai
headline: An LLM judge ensemble sits between planner and controller, gating plans before execution
summary: Robot autonomy research has focused on execution rather than checking whether the actions a planning model proposes are permissible at all. The authors insert an LLM-driven verification layer as middleware between the planning module and the robot's low-level controls, where an LLM-as-a-Judge ensemble combines chain-of-thought reasoning across models in a mixture-of-experts and self-consistency arrangement. Plans are approved, rejected for reformulation, or escalated for human review. The system reaches roughly 85% precision across the three categories and contains 97% of adversarial attacks, with most errors falling at the escalate boundary rather than between accept and reject.
abstract: Advances in advanced artificial intelligence tools have sparked research in robot autonomy, but the development of such systems has largely focused on execution rather than verifying the feasibility actions planning models propose. Like general-purpose LLMs, robotics planning models carry risks: biased toward user-specified goals, they may suggest actions misaligned with scientific ethics, they may be unsafe due to an inability to remember prior safety risks, or they may be vulnerable to adversarial attacks on the autonomy ecosystem. We propose a LLM-driven verification layer between planning and execution to evaluate action permissibility. Our LLM-as-a-Judge ensemble combines chain-of-thought reasoning across models and synthesizes those expert judge outputs, mirroring a combination of a mixture of experts and self-consistency approach. This layer serves as middleware, gating plans from the server's planning module before they reach the MCP server and therefore the robot's low-level controls: plans are approved, rejected for reformulation, or escalated for human review. With this system, we achieve near 85% precision across accept/escalate/reject categories 97% containment of adversarial attacks, with negligible errors between accepting and rejecting tasks, and errors mostly manifesting at the escalate boundary.
notes: Alert: Herbert/Bansal/Tomlin citation. Core - middleware verification layer gating robot plans before they reach low-level control

title: Toward provably safe AI-driven perception and motion planning for robotic manufacturing: A review
authors: Hojun Lee, Yuseop Sim, Junmyoung Jang, Byoungkwon Yoon, Han Gyeom Lee, Hyunmin Park, Chang-Ju Kim, Martin B.G. Jun
matched_interests: Data-driven verification|Verification of visuomotor policies|Safe & robust robot control
headline: Review of provable safety assurance for black-box learned robot systems in manufacturing
summary: Embodied AI and learning-based robotic systems have improved adaptability in manufacturing, but their black-box nature and sensitivity to uncertainty make safety assurance difficult. This review surveys approaches to provably safe AI-driven perception and motion planning in that setting. It is cited across six of the tracked research groups simultaneously, which is unusual and suggests it is functioning as a reference point for the safety-assurance community. The paper is closed-access and the abstract was not retrievable at digest time.
notes: Alert: Tomlin/Bajcsy/Majumdar/Fan/Bansal/Herbert citation. Core - review of provable safety for black-box learned robot systems in manufacturing. NOTE: paywalled, abstract not retrievable at digest time

title: Mining Point-of-No-Return Boundaries in Constrained Dynamical Systems via Counterfactual Auditing
authors: Jia Liu, Jiaxin Luo, Lejun Ai, Yue Wang, Enpeng Lan, Yulong Li, Zongyu Li, Fuxin Zhang, Siyuan Liu, Long Hu, Yixue Hao, Min Chen
matched_interests: Data-driven verification|Uncertainty quantification & failure detection for learned policies
headline: Finds the last recoverable moment before failure becomes unavoidable, separating bad luck from bad decisions
