summary: Outcome metrics like success rate conflate failures that were structurally inevitable with those caused by the policy's decisions. The authors reframe failure diagnosis as recoverability boundary discovery and define the Point-of-No-Return as the last recoverable snapshot before violation becomes unavoidable under an audited intervention class. Counterfactual PoNR Auditing replays snapshots to produce matched counterfactual rollouts, accelerated 3.09x by a neural operator surrogate, and yields Evidence Objects supporting structural-policy decomposition and Failure Atlas mining. On a hydrodynamic control testbed and a bistable system, PoNR precedes observable violation and stays stable under up to 30% multiplicative surrogate noise.
abstract: Safety-critical failures in constrained dynamical environments are often detected only after a violation occurs, while outcome metrics (e.g., success rate, time-to-failure) conflate structural inevitability with decision-induced errors. We formulate failure diagnosis as recoverability boundary discovery and define the Point-of-No-Return (PoNR) as the last recoverable snapshot before violation becomes unavoidable under an audited intervention class. We introduce Counterfactual PoNR Auditing (CPA), a snapshot-replay framework that produces matched counterfactual rollouts and is accelerated by a neural operator surrogate (UNO) for a 3.09x end-to-end speedup. CPA yields Evidence Objects (EOs) that support structural-policy decomposition and enable Failure Atlas mining via contrastive analysis of event sequences within the policy-induced gap. CPA also serves as an offline supervision generator, allowing lightweight predictors to learn early inevitability signals beyond static observational baselines. Experiments on a high-fidelity hydrodynamic control testbed and a canonical bistable system show that PoNR precedes observable violation, remains stable under up to 30% multiplicative surrogate noise, and reduces auditing cost through surrogate-guided search.
notes: Alert: Tomlin/Fan citation. Core - separates structural inevitability from decision-induced error by finding the last recoverable state before violation

title: Critical slowing down for predicting controller induced loss of control in quadrotors
authors: Jasper J. van Beers, Prashant Solanki, Erik-Jan van Kampen, Coen C. de Visser
matched_interests: Data-driven verification|Uncertainty quantification & failure detection for learned policies
headline: Model-free early warning signals predict controller-induced loss of control 0.9 seconds ahead
summary: Borrowing critical slowing down, a phenomenon known to precede critical transitions in ecological and biological systems, the authors build early warning indicators for controller-induced loss of control in quadrotors that require no system model. Evaluated on real flight data from four quadrotors where LOC arises from input-output delays, the scheme forecasts up to 0.9 seconds ahead and beats state-of-the-art recurrent neural network forecasters on both accuracy and reliance on LOC data. Notably it predicts LOC without training on the LOC event itself, and transfers without re-parameterization to a different failure scenario on other quadrotors flying indoors and outdoors.
abstract: We develop a novel forecasting scheme to anticipate controller induced loss of control (LOC) in quadrotors and evaluate it on real LOC flight data from four different quadrotors. For this, early warning signals of LOC are derived using critical slowing down (CSD), a generic phenomenon shown to precede critical transitions across various complex ecological and biological systems. As such, our early warning indicators are generic in the sense that no system models are needed to facilitate forecasts of LOC. The approach is evaluated on real quadrotor flight data wherein LOC occurs due to unstable controller behavior arising from input-output delays. Our approach achieves a time-to-LOC forecast of up to 0.9 seconds before LOC occurs, outperforming state-of-the-art recurrent neural network quadrotor LOC forecasters in terms of detection accuracy and LOC data reliance. In particular, we leverage insights from CSD to accurately predict LOC without using data of the LOC event itself. Going further, we apply our forecasters without any re-parameterization to anticipate a different LOC scenario, quadrotor flyways, that occur on other quadrotors flying both indoors and outdoors. Despite these differences, our approach successfully detects LOC, demonstrating that it can generalize across controller architectures, quadrotors, and LOC scenarios.
notes: Alert: Tomlin/Herbert/Bajcsy/Bansal citation. Core - model-free early warning of controller-induced loss of control, validated on real flight data from four quadrotors

title: Towards Trustworthy Embodied Intelligence: A Systems Framework and Graded Trustworthiness Levels
authors: Xinyu Yang, Tianxing Chen, Honghao Su, Minxuan Wang, Chenze Yu, Zhangzheng Tu, Yue Chen, Yuxiao Huo, Lingfeng Zhang, Yan Huang, et al.
matched_interests: Safe & robust robot control|Uncertainty quantification & failure detection for learned policies
headline: Four-layer framework grading how strongly an embodied system's safety claims are actually evidenced
summary: The authors define trustworthy embodied intelligence as sustained safe success: reliable task execution under environmental and system variation with risk within acceptable bounds. Supporting mechanisms are split into four interdependent layers - model (calibrated uncertainty and safety preferences), system (dependable realization of authorized actions), evidence (evaluation, verification, validation, and assurance arguments), and deployment (runtime monitoring, intervention, controlled updates). Because assumptions and failures propagate across layers, no single layer establishes end-to-end trustworthiness. They propose a non-normative hierarchy grading the strength of bounded deployment claims, aimed at comparative evaluation and eventual standardization.
abstract: Embodied intelligence integrates learned perception and decision making with real-time computation, control, and physical interaction. Because failures can cause immediate physical or operational harm, task completion alone does not establish trustworthiness. We define trustworthy embodied intelligence as the sustained capacity to execute specified tasks reliably under environmental and system variation while maintaining risk within acceptable bounds. We term this objective sustained safe success. Its supporting mechanisms are organized into four interdependent layers. The model layer generates task-competent action proposals with calibrated uncertainty and explicit safety preferences. The system layer realizes authorized actions dependably through integrated sensing, computation, control, hardware safeguards, fault containment, and fallback. The evidence layer substantiates bounded claims through evaluation, verification, validation, traceability, and structured assurance arguments. The deployment layer maintains claim validity through runtime monitoring, authority management, intervention, incident response, and controlled updates. Because assumptions and failures propagate across these layers, neither model capability, isolated safeguards, nor benchmark performance alone can establish end-to-end trustworthiness. Drawing on embodied AI, robotics, control, dependable computing, distributed systems, and autonomous driving, we further propose a non-normative hierarchy of trustworthiness levels. This hierarchy grades the strength of bounded deployment claims across task capability, safety, system assurance, operational governance, and supporting evidence, providing a basis for bounded deployment, comparative evaluation, research prioritization, and future standardization.
notes: Alert: Tomlin/Herbert/Bansal/Majumdar citation. High - four-layer trustworthiness framework with an explicit evidence layer for verification and assurance arguments

title: The Case for Physical AI Safety
authors: Kaylene Stocking, Bear Haon
headline: $18.7B into robot foundation models, roughly zero into their safety
summary: An agenda-setting report from the newly launched Physical AI Safety Institute arguing that robotics is shifting from narrow task-specific control to large general-reasoning robot foundation models, and that the safety side of that shift is drastically underfunded. The authors count over $18.7B raised to build RFMs against dedicated safety funding that rounds to zero, a capabilities-to-safety ratio they say is unmatched elsewhere in frontier AI. They argue physical embodiment amplifies AI risk by giving misaligned or misused models direct causal access to the world. Their claim is that the area is important, neglected, and tractable, since techniques from classical robotics and non-physical foundation models can be adapted.
abstract: [Report executive summary, verbatim] Robotics is undergoing a paradigm shift: from narrow single-task perception, planning, and control, to large general-reasoning robot foundation models (RFMs). The upcoming era is that of Physical AI. RFMs take plain language instructions as input (tidy the kitchen, unload the truck) and produce physical navigation/manipulation commands to achieve the task. Companies have raised over $18.7B to build these AI models, some with the explicit goal of realizing embodied AGI. Dedicated funding for their safety, to our knowledge, rounds to zero. We are not aware of a capabilities-to-safety ratio this lopsided anywhere else in frontier AI. Physical AI safety risks include malicious use, misalignment, accidental harm, emotional dependency, privacy violations, and broader societal risks such as inequality, malicious development, and power centralization. Physical embodiment is an AI risk amplifier, giving misaligned or misused foundation models direct causal access to the world and facilitating anthropomorphization. Physical AI safety research is important, neglected, and tractable: The ability of RFMs to physically interact with the world around them introduces serious new risks compared to non-embodied AI. Since there are very strong economic incentives to widely deploy RFMs, these risks indicate that physical AI safety will become very important in the near future. While a rich safety literature exists for narrow task-based robotics, very few techniques exist to interpret, align, and control RFMs: physical AI safety research is neglected. However, there are many promising approaches in both classic robotics and in non-physical foundation models that could be adapted to RFMs, suggesting that this research is also tractable. To mitigate plausible near- and long-term risks, we believe that more people should be researching methods to interpret, align, and control RFMs. To catalyze this future, we are launching The Physical AI Safety Institute.
notes: Alert: Tomlin/Bajcsy citation. Core - agenda-setting report arguing verification of robot foundation models is important, neglected, and tractable. NOTE: institute report, no formal abstract; stored text is the verbatim executive summary

title: Failing Gracefully: Mitigating Impact of Inevitable Robot Failures
authors: Duc M. Nguyen, Saad A. Ghani, Andrew Marshall, Allison Andreyev, Gregory J. Stein, Xuesu Xiao
matched_interests: Safe & robust robot control|Uncertainty quantification & failure detection for learned policies
headline: Plan for the failures you cannot prevent: probability times severity as a safety objective
summary: Some robot failures are inevitable, so the authors shift the question from preventing them to bounding their consequences. Their safety formulation evaluates both the probability of impactful interactions between a failing robot and surrounding humans, pets, and objects, and the severity of those outcomes. Quantifying impact per entity lets a planner trade safety against task efficiency explicitly. They also release FailBench, a MuJoCo framework for studying robot-environment interaction under sensing and actuator failure modes.
abstract: Service robots operate in household environments shared with humans, pets, and everyday objects, where they are highly susceptible to failures such as software crashes, hardware degradation, or unpredictable interactions. While roboticists strive to minimize failures, some remain inevitable, making it critical to mitigate their potential consequences for safe and reliable deployment. This paper introduces a novel safety formulation that evaluates both the probability of impactful interactions between robots and surrounding entities during failures, and the severity of their outcomes. By quantifying the impact of failures on different entities, our approach enables robots to make informed planning decisions that balance safety with task efficiency. To support systematic evaluation, we also present FailBench, a MuJoCo-based simulation framework for studying robot-environment interactions under diverse failure modes, including sensing issues and actuator malfunctions. Together, our safety formulation and FailBench provide a foundation for developing safer and more robust motion plans and learned policies in real-world household environments.
notes: Alert: Tomlin/Bajcsy/Bansal/Herbert. High - safety formulation over both probability and severity of failure outcomes, with a simulation benchmark

title: Shielding for Higher-Order Safety
authors: Filip Cano, Thomas A. Henzinger, Konstantin Kueffner
matched_interests: Safe & robust robot control|Signal Temporal Logic (STL)
headline: Runtime shields that respect speed, force, and jerk limits, not just collision predicates
summary: Classical safety shields are synthesized for state predicates, treating the current physical state as safe or unsafe, which is too coarse for cyber-physical systems that must also respect speed regulations, acceleration-induced force limits, and jerk limits. The authors define differential safety properties using finite differences over a discretized state space and reduce shield synthesis to an ordinary safety game over a history state space. They prove that a shield for an order-k property needs exactly k past states and that this memory is necessary. An iterative procedure solves derivative constraints in increasing order, pruning the state space at each step so synthesis avoids exploring regions already known unsafe.
abstract: Safety shields are runtime enforcement mechanisms that restrict the actions of a controller to guarantee safety. Classical shields are usually synthesised for state predicates: the current physical state is either safe or unsafe, and the shield disables precisely those actions that can force the system into an unsafe state in the future. In many cyber-physical applications this view is too coarse. A vehicle approaching an obstacle should not only avoid collision, but also respect speed regulations, force limits induced by acceleration, and jerk limits to prevent injuries. From a physical perspective, these requirements are predicated over the derivatives of the state. This paper develops a finite-state safety-game construction for such high-order smoothness constraints. We define differential safety properties using finite differences over a discretised state space, characterise their expressiveness, and reduce shield synthesis to an ordinary safety game over a history state space. We give a synthesis algorithm whose shields store exactly k past states for properties of order k and prove that this memory is necessary. We describe an iterative synthesis procedure for a maximally permissive shield that operates over hierarchies of derivative constraints. The algorithm solves constraints iteratively in increasing order and uses the solution at each iteration to prune the state space for the next constraint. This makes shield synthesis more efficient in practice, as the algorithm refrains from exploring large regions of the state space that are known to be unsafe.
notes: Alert: Bansal/Lindemann. High - runtime shields for constraints over state derivatives, not just state predicates

title: Provably Safe Controller Synthesis via Learning-Assisted Vector Barrier Certificates Generation
authors: Mengxin Ren, Zhengfeng Yang, Xia Zeng, Zhiming Liu
venue: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems
matched_interests: Data-driven verification|Control Barrier Functions (CBFs)|Safe & robust robot control
headline: Verify a learned barrier certificate instead of synthesizing one, keeping non-convex constraints intact
summary: Learning-based controllers perform well in training and simulation but lack the formal guarantees needed for safety-critical deployment. The authors use learning to propose candidate vector barrier certificates, which are more expressive than single barrier certificates, and then formally verify them. Verifying a learned candidate rather than directly synthesizing a verified one lowers computational complexity. Unlike prior vector BC methods that relax the non-convex constraints and shrink the feasible set, this approach handles the original constraints directly.
abstract: The design of controllers for safety-critical systems is an important research topic, particularly in the context of synthesizing controllers with formal safety guarantees, which remains a challenging problem. In recent years, machine learning techniques have been increasingly applied to various control tasks to achieve strong performance in training and simulation. However, these methods often lack the formal guarantees required for deployment in safety-critical applications. This paper leverages learning-based techniques to support the synthesis of safe controllers with provable guarantees. While candidate control policies can be generated via diverse methods, including reinforcement learning, our primary technical contribution is a learning-assisted framework for synthesizing vector barrier certificates (BCs) and formally verifying the safety of the resulting controllers. Vector BCs provide greater expressiveness than traditional single barrier certificates for safety verification. Compared with existing approaches to vector BC synthesis, the proposed method offers two main advantages. First, rather than directly synthesizing a verified vector BC, our method verifies a learned candidate vector BC, which results in lower computational complexity. Second, previous methods have relaxed the non-convex vector BC constraints, thereby reducing the feasible solution space, while our approach is capable of handling the original constraints without such relaxations. Experimental results on a variety of benchmark problems demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method and clarify its current empirical scope.
notes: Alert: Lindemann. Core - verifies a learned candidate vector barrier certificate rather than synthesizing a verified one, keeping the original non-convex constraints

title: Robust data-driven MPC with analytic probabilistic safety barriers
authors: Mahmood Mazare, Hossein Ramezani
headline: RKHS error bounds replace intractable geometric terminal sets with analytic safety margins
summary: Robust safety for unknown nonlinear systems usually requires computing geometric invariant sets that scale badly with dimension. Safe KDPC learns both a control Lyapunov function and a robust control barrier function from offline data using kernel methods with formal RKHS error bounds. The key contribution is analytic Lipschitz-based safety margins that explicitly decompose total uncertainty into epistemic model error and aleatoric disturbance, letting a convex analytically defined region of attraction stand in for the terminal set while preserving recursive feasibility. Practical stability and forward safety invariance hold with probability at least 1-delta, and simulations show reduced conservatism versus nominal and robust tube MPC under distribution shift.
abstract: Ensuring robust safety for unknown nonlinear systems is a fundamental challenge, typically requiring the computation of complex geometric invariant sets that scale poorly with dimension. Addressing this, we propose Safe Kernel-based Data-driven Predictive Control (Safe KDPC), a geometric terminal set-free Robust Model Predictive Control architecture. We leverage kernel-based learning with formal error bounds derived from Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) theory to learn both a Control Lyapunov Function (CLF) and a Robust Control Barrier Function (RCBF) from offline data. A key contribution is the derivation of analytic Lipschitz-based safety margins that explicitly decompose total uncertainty into epistemic model error and aleatoric disturbance. These margins allow us to replace the computationally prohibitive geometric terminal set with a convex, analytically defined region of attraction that ensures recursive feasibility. We provide rigorous proofs for practical stability and forward safety invariance that hold with probability at least 1-delta, conditioned on our probabilistic model error bounds. The proposed framework eliminates the need for Minkowski sum computations while guaranteeing robust constraint satisfaction. Comparative simulations against both nominal and Robust Tube MPC baselines demonstrate reduced conservatism and maintained safety under distributional shift, validating the advantage of the proposed terminal set-free architecture.
notes: Alert: Tomlin citation. Core - RKHS error bounds yield analytic safety margins that replace geometric terminal sets for unknown nonlinear systems

title: How Much Do Your Models Disagree? Adaptive MPC Safety from Ensemble Uncertainty
authors: Ali Baheri
venue: IEEE Open Journal of Control Systems
matched_interests: Uncertainty quantification & failure detection for learned policies|Data-driven verification|Safe & robust robot control
headline: Ensemble disagreement becomes a state-dependent safety margin, cutting violations 76%
summary: A fixed safety margin is too conservative where a learned dynamics model is accurate and too aggressive where it is not. EA-MPC propagates a covariance capturing both process noise and ensemble disagreement, then inflates obstacle constraints using one of three concentration inequalities - Chebyshev, Cantelli, or Gaussian - trading distributional assumptions against tightness. Per-step margins lift to trajectory level via a Bonferroni union bound and a steady-state approximation. The distribution-free bound cuts constraint violations by 76% versus certainty-equivalent control, and the method matches well-tuned fixed margins on an underactuated quadrotor without manual margin tuning.
abstract: Prediction errors of learned dynamics models vary across the state space, so a fixed safety margin is either too conservative where the model is accurate or too aggressive where it is not. We propose Ensemble-Aware Model Predictive Control (EA-MPC), which turns ensemble disagreement into state-dependent safety margins: it propagates a covariance capturing process noise and model disagreement and inflates obstacle constraints with one of three concentration inequalities: Chebyshev, Cantelli (tighter through one-sided geometry, at the same second-moment assumption), and Gaussian (tightest at these risk levels, under a distributional assumption). The covariance-bound schedule stays bounded, and we lift the per-step margins to the trajectory level via a Bonferroni correction (a union bound given per-step margins) and a steady-state correction (a practical approximation, conservative in our runs). On benchmarks with nonlinear dynamics and systematic mismatch, the bounds trace a cost-safety frontier: the distribution-free bound cuts constraint violations by 76% versus certainty-equivalent control, while the tighter margins reduce cost at the expense of more violations, under mild aggregate undercoverage. We compare EA MPC against a data-driven quantile-tube baseline and validate it on an underactuated quadrotor, matching well-tuned fixed margins without manually tuning a fixed obstacle margin.
notes: Alert: Lindemann citation. Core - converts ensemble disagreement into state-dependent safety margins with three concentration inequalities

title: Topological Feasibility Guarantees for Differentiable Predictive Control
authors: Guangyu Wu, Jan Drgona
headline: Deterministic feasibility certificates for learned MPC policies, no online safety filter needed
summary: Differentiable predictive control approximates explicit MPC policies offline and is far cheaper than online optimization, but its feasibility guarantees have been probabilistic or delegated to online safety filters. The authors give deterministic guarantees via a topological analysis of the induced reachable safe set, exploiting the fact that differentiable dynamics are embedded directly in DPC's computational graph. They propose a self-supervised offline policy learning strategy using a control-barrier-function proxy loss, which both improves training and enables strict feasibility guarantees from finitely many training samples. Simulations show empirical constraint violations decreasing monotonically to zero as sample size grows - certificates the authors argue are structurally unattainable for black-box RL or supervised approximate MPC.
abstract: Differentiable predictive control (DPC), a self-supervised learning approach for approximating explicit model predictive control (MPC) policies, offers significant computational advantages over online optimization-based MPC. However, feasibility guarantees, a core requirement for safe control, are currently provided either probabilistically or via online safety filters. The lack of rigorous feasibility guarantees for offline policy optimization remains an open problem. This paper establishes deterministic feasibility guarantees for DPC using a novel topological analysis of the induced reachable safe set, without requiring online safety filters. By exploiting the inherent model-based nature of DPC, in which differentiable system dynamics are embedded directly into the computational graph, we analyze the properties of the learned control policies and the corresponding system states from topological and geometric perspectives. Inspired by our theoretical analysis, we propose a novel self-supervised offline policy learning strategy that utilizes a proxy loss with Control Barrier Functions (CBFs). Crucially, these properties not only significantly improve policy training but also enable the derivation of strict, deterministic feasibility guarantees from a finite number of training samples. Extensive closed-loop simulations validate our theoretical findings, demonstrating that the empirical constraint violations monotonically decrease to zero as the training sample size increases. Ultimately, this work illustrates that DPC policy optimization yields formal safety certificates that are structurally unattainable with conventional black-box methods, e.g., reinforcement learning (RL) or supervised learning-based approximate MPC, thereby providing a new perspective on feasibility guarantees in learning-based control.
notes: Alert: Lindemann/Tomlin/Herbert/Bansal citation. Core - deterministic feasibility certificates for learned explicit-MPC policies from finite training samples

title: Expanding Safe Sets with Learning-Based Barrier Functions and Reachability
authors: Trevor Matthews, Mahesh Kumar A.R., Azra Begzadic, Sander Tonkens, Zhirui Dai, Nikolay Atanasov, Jorge Cortes, Sylvia Herbert
matched_interests: Control Barrier Functions (CBFs)|Hamilton-Jacobi reachability|Safe & robust robot control
headline: Learn a barrier from noisy LiDAR, then let reachability make it formally valid
summary: GP-CBF learns a smooth conservative estimate of the signed distance function from noisy LiDAR using Gaussian process regression and a Bayesian Hilbert map in real time. That learned SDF serves as a candidate control barrier function, which Hamilton-Jacobi reachability analysis then formally refines into a valid control barrier value function. The value function updates online as new measurements arrive, progressively expanding the safe set while retaining probabilistic safety guarantees. Simulation and hardware experiments on a mobile robot in clutter show the approach outperforming existing baselines.
abstract: This paper presents GP-CBF, a learning-based framework for synthesizing and continuously adapting a robust control barrier value function for safe robot navigation in unknown environments. The approach first learns a smooth, conservative estimate of the signed distance function from noisy LiDAR data using Gaussian process regression and a Bayesian Hilbert map in real time. This learned signed distance function serves as a candidate control barrier function, which is then formally refined using Hamilton-Jacobi reachability analysis to generate a valid control barrier value function. The resulting value function is updated online as new sensor measurements are added, enabling progressive expansion of the safe set while maintaining probabilistic safety guarantees. The efficacy of our approach is validated through both simulation and hardware experiments on a mobile robot traversing cluttered environments, ensuring safety and outperforming existing baselines.
notes: Alert: Tomlin/Lindemann/Bansal/Herbert. High - Herbert group; learns a signed distance function from LiDAR then refines it into a valid CBVF via HJ reachability

title: A smooth compositional framework for learned control barrier functions with provable safety guarantees
authors: Yang Yang, Liang Xu, Xiaofan Wang
matched_interests: Control Barrier Functions (CBFs)|Controller composition|Safe & robust robot control
headline: Smoothly fusing local learned barriers has a hidden failure mode; here is the fix
summary: The authors address two problems in composing learned control barrier functions: the absence of out-of-distribution safety guarantees for learned function approximators, and a previously unidentified failure mode arising from smooth composition itself. They first introduce a safe-by-design paradigm where a structured network with a quadratic penalty term provides provably conservative estimates in unexplored regions. They then formally identify and analyse a weight interference term that emerges when local functions are smoothly fused, derive an analytical bound on it, and build a state-dependent safety margin that provably guarantees forward invariance. Simulation shows zero collisions and smoother control than non-smooth baselines.
abstract: This paper develops a rigorous compositional framework for provably safe controllers in unknown environments. We address two key challenges: the lack of out-of-distribution safety guarantees for learned function approximators, and a previously unidentified failure mode in smooth composition. We first introduce a safe-by-design paradigm for learning local Control Barrier Functions, where a structured neural network with a quadratic penalty term provides provable conservative estimates in unexplored regions. Having established local safety, we then formally identify, analyse, and compensate for a weight interference term that emerges from the smooth fusion of local functions. We derive an analytical bound on this term and construct a robust, state-dependent safety margin that provably guarantees forward invariance of the safe set. The framework is validated in simulation, achieving zero collision rates in the evaluated scenarios and generating significantly smoother, more efficient control actions than non-smooth baselines.
notes: Alert: Bajcsy/Bansal/Fan/Herbert/Lindemann. High - identifies a previously unnoticed failure mode when smoothly fusing local learned CBFs

title: Learning Input-Constrained Funnel Controllers from State Trajectory Data
authors: Panagiotis S. Trakas, Omid Mirzaeedodangeh, Lars Lindemann
headline: Learns both the performance spec and the controller from state trajectories, no expert actions needed
summary: State trajectories from an expert controller implicitly encode feasible performance attributes and input limits, and the authors exploit this directly. Their optimization-based framework jointly learns a performance funnel matching the observed transient and steady-state behavior, and a feedback controller enforcing that specification under hard input constraints. Unlike imitation learning, the method needs no control input data and never reconstructs the expert policy; it combines nominal model compensation with a learned state-dependent feedback gain. They handle the resulting non-convex synthesis with a feasibility-driven active-set procedure and prove a semi-global actuator-authority certificate plus a local data-driven certificate near densely demonstrated trajectories.
abstract: Designing feedback controllers that satisfy predefined performance specifications while enforcing hard input constraints is a challenging task. Our work is motivated by the idea that state trajectory data, e.g., obtained from an expert controller, often implicitly encode feasible performance attributes and input limitations. We propose an optimization-based framework that uses state trajectory data to jointly learn: (i) a performance funnel that mimics the transient and steady-state behavior encoded within the observed trajectories, and (ii) a feedback controller that enforces the learned performance specifications under hard input constraints. Unlike imitation learning methods, the proposed approach does not rely on control input data and does not reconstruct an expert policy. Instead, it synthesizes a prescribed performance controller by combining nominal model compensation with a learned state-dependent feedback gain. The resulting synthesis problem is nonconvex, for which we develop a feasibility-driven active-set synthesis procedure. Finally, we establish two complementary guarantees: a semi-global conservative actuator-authority-based certificate for prescribed performance and input satisfaction, and a local data-driven certificate ensuring these properties near sufficiently dense demonstrated trajectories.
notes: Alert: Lindemann new articles. Core - Lindemann group; learns performance funnel and controller jointly from state trajectories without any control input data

title: Safe Learning Predictive Control for Ego-World Robotic Systems
authors: Davide Valenti, Giuseppe Notarstefano
matched_interests: World models for robotics|Safe & robust robot control
headline: Learn the other robot's unknown policy online, then plan safely against your posterior over it
summary: SOWL-MPC targets a setting the authors call the ego-world robotic framework, where the control policy of the surrounding world robot is unknown and the ego robot must learn it from data to maneuver safely. Sparse Variational Gaussian Processes infer a posterior over the latent world policy from noisy state measurements alone, updated on streaming data via Online Variational Conditioning. That posterior is propagated through the nonlinear world dynamics by approximate moment propagation and fed to an uncertainty-aware MPC. Real-time feasibility and safety are demonstrated in ROS 2 Monte Carlo experiments and validated on real hardware in an indoor arena.
abstract: Safe autonomous navigation in shared environments requires the ability to anticipate and react to the latent behaviors of surrounding robots. In this paper, we propose SOWL-MPC, a safe learning-based predictive control strategy for a novel scenario, which we name ego-world robotic framework. In this setting, the control policy of the world robot is unknown and the ego exploits data to learn it and perform safe maneuvers. The proposed architecture combines an online learning mechanism based on Sparse Variational Gaussian Processes (SVGPs) with a receding-horizon control scheme. Relying solely on noisy state measurements, our approach infers a posterior distribution over the latent world policy, which is updated on streaming data via Online Variational Conditioning (OVC). The learned policy is propagated through the nonlinear world dynamics using an approximate moment propagation scheme, and fed to an uncertainty-aware Model Predictive Control (MPC), thus enabling safe maneuvering of the ego robot. The real-time feasibility and safety guarantees of SOWL-MPC are demonstrated through extensive Monte Carlo virtual experiments in ROS 2, and validated on real-world robotic hardware in an indoor arena.
notes: Alert: Tomlin. Core - learns the unknown control policy of another robot online and feeds the posterior into uncertainty-aware MPC

title: Adaptive Stability-Constrained Neural Differential Equations for Controlled Dynamical Systems with Unknown Inputs
authors: Syed Pouladi
headline: Contraction-constrained neural ODEs bound how fast learned dynamics diverge under unseen inputs
summary: Learned vector fields accumulate error rapidly when rolled out under inputs unlike those seen in training. AS-NDE jointly learns a nominal vector field and a state- and input-dependent Riemannian metric, enforcing positive definiteness by construction while a sampled differential inequality penalizes violations of a prescribed contraction rate. The authors derive an incremental input-to-state bound showing trajectory separation decays exponentially up to gains set by control and disturbance differences, explicitly accounting for the time derivative of the input-dependent metric that heuristic stability regularizers typically omit. Note that the manuscript openly labels all numerical curves as illustrative synthetic placeholders pending the prescribed experiments.
abstract: Continuous-time neural models are attractive for identifying nonlinear systems, but a small one-step error can grow rapidly when a learned vector field is rolled out under inputs that differ from those used for training. This paper develops an adaptive stability-constrained neural differential equation (AS-NDE) for systems with measured controls and unmatched, unknown perturbations. The nominal vector field and a state-input-dependent Riemannian metric are learned jointly. Positive definiteness is enforced by construction, while a sampled differential inequality penalizes violations of a prescribed contraction rate. An incremental input-to-state bound is derived: the distance between two trajectories decays exponentially up to gains determined by differences in their controls and disturbances. The statement explicitly accounts for the time derivative of an input-dependent metric, a term that is easily omitted in heuristic stability regularizers. We give a reproducible evaluation protocol for a forced Duffing oscillator and a permanent-magnet synchronous motor (PMSM) model. Because no measured data or executed training runs accompany this draft, all numerical curves and tables are clearly identified as illustrative synthetic placeholders; their PGFPlots coordinates are embedded in the source for direct replacement. The resulting manuscript is intended as a technically consistent starting point, not as evidence of empirical superiority before the prescribed experiments are run.
notes: Alert: Fan citation. High - contraction-constrained neural ODEs with an incremental ISS bound. CAUTION: the authors state all numerical results are synthetic placeholders pending experiments

title: Certified Feedforward Tracking for Unknown Nonlinear Systems via Invertible Neural Networks
authors: Berk Altiner, Rajasree Sarkar, Arunava Banerjee, Zongxuan Sun, Kenneth Kim
headline: Invertible surrogates turn tracking-error certification into a conformal prediction problem
summary: Certifying data-driven feedforward control for periodic tracking of unknown nonlinear systems normally requires solving a non-convex inversion problem that introduces its own errors. The authors adopt an invertible neural network as the system surrogate, which bypasses inversion entirely and reduces tracking-error certification to a surrogate modeling problem. Conformal prediction then supplies finite-sample probabilistic guarantees on surrogate modeling error, which propagate through a derived tracking-error bound to give marginal certificates on feedforward tracking error. The method is demonstrated on a DC-motor-driven mechanical load with nonlinear friction.
abstract: In this paper, we address the certification of datadriven feedforward control for periodic tracking of unknown nonlinear systems under partial state measurements. To this end, we adopt an invertible neural network (INN) as a surrogate for the unknown system. This choice allows us to bypass solving a nonconvex inversion problem, eliminating the associated inversion errors and reducing tracking error certification to a surrogate modeling problem. We then apply conformal prediction to provide finite-sample probabilistic guarantees on the surrogate modeling error which, through the derived tracking error bound, yield marginal certificates on feedforward tracking error. Finally, we demonstrate the approach on a DC-motor-driven mechanical load with nonlinear friction.
notes: Alert: Lindemann citation. Core - invertible network surrogate reduces tracking-error certification to a conformal surrogate-modeling problem

title: Particle-Based Conformal Prediction for Contact-Aware Uncertainty Calibration in Stratified Configuration Spaces
authors: Luis Marques, Kristian Popov, Dmitry Berenson
matched_interests: Conformal prediction|Uncertainty quantification & failure detection for learned policies
headline: Conformal prediction that stays calibrated when contact collapses the state distribution onto manifolds
summary: When a robot contacts an obstacle, the distribution over its future configurations can become multimodal, disjoint, or supported on manifolds of lower intrinsic dimension than the configuration space, which breaks standard uncertainty estimates. CaPTURe is a geometry-aware conformal prediction algorithm producing probabilistically valid prediction regions from particle-based models of arbitrary fidelity. Its calibration procedure captures how motion uncertainty differs between contact-rich and contactless motion, giving sufficient coverage in both regimes. On a marble labyrinth and tight-tolerance peg-in-hole insertion, it hits the specified coverage in and out of contact and improves task success by up to 30 absolute points over the best baseline.
abstract: Reliable uncertainty representation is essential for deploying autonomous systems that interact with their environment, as robots must reason about how uncertainty arising from both stochasticity and model mismatch is impacted by contacts with obstacles (e.g., when navigating through a cluttered environment or inserting a part into an assembly). We propose Calibrated Particle-sets for Trans-dimensional Uncertainty Representation (CaPTURe), a geometry-aware, conformal prediction-based algorithm that generates probabilistically valid prediction regions of the unknown future system configuration using particle-based models of arbitrary fidelity. While calibrated uncertainty predictions are essential for safe and efficient planning, analytical or learned motion models are often inaccurate - due to limited data, simplifying assumptions, unmodeled effects, etc. - which can lead to unsafe executions or task failure. Additionally, when a robot contacts an obstacle, the distribution of its future configurations can become multimodal or disjoint, or lie along manifolds of lower intrinsic dimension than the space of possible robot configurations. Our method uses a calibration dataset of system transitions to locally calibrate motion uncertainty estimates, constructing regions guaranteed to contain the future robot configuration at a user-set probability. Our calibration procedure captures how motion uncertainty varies between contact-rich and contactless motions, leading to sufficient coverage in both cases. We evaluate our method on two simulated planning tasks: controlling a marble around a labyrinth and performing tight-tolerance peg-in-hole insertion with a manipulator. Compared to relevant baselines, CaPTURe achieves the user-specified coverage requirement both in and out of contact and achieves up to a 30% absolute improvement in task success rate over the best baseline.
notes: Alert: Lindemann citation. High - conformal prediction that stays calibrated when contact makes the future-state distribution multimodal or lower-dimensional

title: CoCoNav: Conformal Control for Safe Robot Navigation in Crowds
authors: Cheng Guo, Mingzhe Ni, Zheng Liang, Yihu Ling, Yuan Hu, Michele Caprio, Daniele Pucci, Wei Pan
headline: Relax-then-verify keeps MPC feasible while still certifying against conformal pedestrian bounds
summary: Treating conservative uncertainty sets as hard MPC constraints can make the solver infeasible, while treating forecasts as exact produces unsafe or oscillatory behavior. CoCoNav pairs a horizon-specific conformal proportional-integral controller, which adapts trajectory-error bounds to regulate long-run empirical coverage, with a relax-then-verify planner. Nominal trajectories come from soft-constrained MPC and are certified separately, together with contingency maneuvers, against the calibrated bounds before execution. Simulations and quadruped experiments show a favorable balance among collision avoidance, task success, and navigation efficiency. Widely cited across five of the tracked groups this cycle.
abstract: Safe and efficient robot navigation in crowds requires anticipating pedestrian motion despite uncertain and potentially shifting prediction errors. Existing reactive methods can produce oscillatory behavior, while predictive planners often treat forecasts as exact or rely on restrictive error models. Incorporating conservative uncertainty sets as hard constraints can also render model predictive control (MPC) infeasible. We propose CoCoNav, a crowd-navigation framework that combines online conformal calibration with runtime-certified planning. A horizon-specific conformal proportional-integral controller adapts trajectory-error bounds to regulate long-run empirical coverage, enabling the framework to respond to changing prediction errors. A relax-then-verify planner preserves solver feasibility by generating nominal trajectories with soft-constrained MPC and separately certifying them, together with contingency maneuvers, against the calibrated bounds before execution. Simulations and quadruped experiments show that CoCoNav achieves a favorable balance among collision avoidance, task success, and navigation efficiency relative to the evaluated baselines.
notes: Alert: Herbert/Bansal/Tomlin/Lindemann/Bajcsy citation. High - relax-then-verify keeps MPC feasible while still certifying against calibrated conformal bounds

title: Conformal Constraint Tightening for Chance-Constrained Motion Planning with Unknown Dynamics
authors: Shubham Natraj, Bruno Sinopoli, Yiannis Kantaros
headline: Planner-agnostic conformal tightening restores task guarantees when the true dynamics are unknown
summary: Sampling-based planners and deep RL both give task-completion guarantees only with respect to a nominal model or simulator, guarantees that evaporate when the true dynamics are unknown. The authors contribute a planner-agnostic constraint-tightening procedure that equips any existing planner with a probabilistic task-completion guarantee on the true system. Conformal prediction supplies a probabilistic bound on nominal-to-true trajectory deviation across a distribution of planning problems, and planning constraints are tightened by that bound. They show solving the tightened problem under the nominal model is sufficient for solving the original problem on the true system with prescribed probability.
abstract: Motion planning algorithms compute control sequences that drive autonomous robots to goal regions while avoiding unsafe states. Existing methods, from sampling-based planning to deep reinforcement learning, typically provide task-completion guarantees only with respect to a nominal model or simulator, which may be invalidated when the true dynamics are unknown or difficult to model accurately. This letter addresses this limitation for systems with unknown dynamics and an available approximate nominal model, contributing a planner-agnostic constraint-tightening procedure that equips existing planners with a probabilistic task-completion guarantee on the true system. We leverage conformal prediction to provide a probabilistic bound on the nominal-to-true trajectory deviation over a distribution of planning problems. We tighten the planning constraints using that bound, and show that solving the tightened problem under the nominal model is a sufficient condition for solving the original problem on the true system with a prescribed probability. We validate the theoretical guarantees empirically and demonstrate substantially improved task completion relative to nominal-model planning.
notes: Alert: Tomlin/Lindemann/Majumdar citation. Core - planner-agnostic conformal tightening restores task-completion guarantees on the true system

title: Directional Conformal Uncertainty Quantification from Learned Model Discrepancy
authors: Cesare Donati, Fabrizio Dabbene, Martina Mammarella
matched_interests: Conformal prediction|Uncertainty quantification & failure detection for learned policies
headline: Asymmetric conformal sets that penalize errors less when they match the learned discrepancy
summary: Physics-based predictors used in control are chosen for synthesis and real-time compatibility rather than accuracy, so their error combines process noise with a state-dependent discrepancy. The authors learn that discrepancy and use it to define an asymmetric nonconformity score, penalizing errors consistent with the learned discrepancy less than equally large errors in the opposite direction. The resulting sets stay in the nominal model's error coordinates and are physics-consistent, containing a ball at the origin. The construction is agnostic to the discrepancy model, preserves finite-sample marginal validity under exchangeability, and provably narrows intervals over a characterizable state-input region.
abstract: We propose a conformal prediction framework for quantifying the error of physics-based predictors used in control, where simple models are preferred for synthesis, certification, and real-time use. Because these models are selected for compatibility with the intended application rather than for maximal predictive accuracy, their error combines process noise with a state-dependent discrepancy. A data-driven discrepancy estimate defines an asymmetric nonconformity score: errors consistent with the learned discrepancy are penalized less than equally large in the opposite direction. The sets remain in the nominal model's error coordinates and are physics-consistent, i.e., they contain a ball at the origin. The construction is agnostic to the discrepancy model (kernel, neural-network, or other), preserves finite-sample marginal validity under exchangeability, and provably narrows the interval over a characterizable state-input region. We further show that, for RKHS models, the power function provides a local confidence measure for adaptive score design and we extend the construction to the multivariate case via a Minkowski-gauge score yielding a jointly calibrated disturbance set.
notes: Alert: Lindemann citation. High - asymmetric nonconformity scores that exploit a learned discrepancy model while staying physics-consistent

title: Conformal Risk-Adaptive Navigation for Mobile Robot in Crowded Environments
authors: Weishu Zhan, Yichi Zhang, Philip Guodong Zhao
headline: Online conformal calibration feeds dynamic barrier functions for crowd navigation under distribution shift
summary: CRA-MPC combines probabilistic ensemble learning with online adaptive conformal calibration to adjust safety boundaries in real time as crowd dynamics shift away from training conditions. A Probabilistic Ensemble Neural Network handles long-horizon waypoint selection while an Adaptive Conformal Unit calibrates short-term safety, feeding uncertainty estimates into dynamic control barrier functions inside risk-adaptive MPC. In moderate crowds with perception noise it reaches 92% success, ten points above state-of-the-art learning methods, and cuts collisions from 13% to 5%. Solver feasibility stays at 97% with no warm-up period required.
abstract: Mobile robots navigating in dense crowds experience performance degradation under distribution shifts between training and deployment. We propose Conformal Risk-Adaptive Model Predictive Control (CRA-MPC), the first method combining probabilistic ensemble learning with online adaptive conformal calibration to achieve real-time safety boundary adjustment in dynamic crowds. Our hierarchical framework integrates a Probabilistic Ensemble Neural Network (PENN) for long-horizon waypoint selection with an Adaptive Conformal Unit (ACU) for short-term safety calibration, feeding uncertainty estimates into dynamic control barrier functions within risk-adaptive MPC. In moderate crowds with perception noise, CRA-MPC achieves 92% success rate - 10% higher than state-of-the-art learning methods - while reducing collision rates from 13% to 5%. Under severe uncertainty, CRA-MPC maintains operational capability and outperforms all baselines fail infeasibility or excessive collisions. The framework achieves 97% solver feasibility without requiring warm-up, enabling immediate adaptation to changing crowd dynamics.
notes: Alert: Tomlin citation. High - online conformal calibration feeding dynamic CBFs inside risk-adaptive MPC, no warm-up needed

title: Simultaneous Coverage and Efficiency Guarantee in Online Conformal Prediction
authors: Rahul Vaze
headline: Adaptive conformal inference has three structural holes; this closes them
summary: The author identifies three limitations of adaptive conformal inference and its variants: guarantees control only signed long-run coverage error, so sustained miscoverage can be masked by later compensation; nothing constrains prediction-set size, so validity is achievable trivially with useless intervals; and existing efficiency guarantees compare against a fixed hindsight predictor, a benchmark that loses meaning once the distribution shifts. A unified online-learning framework controls absolute non-cancelling coverage violation and set efficiency against a dynamically evolving benchmark. Exploiting the fact that the standard ACI update is projected online gradient descent on the pinball loss, the fully adversarial case yields simultaneous guarantees with no distributional or convexity assumptions, and the stochastic case gets a rate-optimal sliding-window quantile tracker.
abstract: Adaptive conformal inference (ACI) of Gibbs and Candes and its variants are the standard approach to online conformal prediction under distribution shift, but they suffer from three fundamental limitations. First, their guarantees control only the signed long-run coverage error: persistent miscoverage in one direction can be masked by compensating errors later, so a method can satisfy the theoretical guarantee while being badly wrong for extended periods. Second, existing guarantees say nothing about prediction-set size, so validity can be achieved trivially at the cost of unduly wide prediction sets. Third, the efficiency guarantees that do exist compare against a fixed predictor chosen in hindsight, a benchmark that becomes increasingly less meaningful once the data-generating distribution shifts, since the very notion of an optimal threshold then changes over time. We consider a unified online learning framework that simultaneously controls absolute, non-cancelling coverage violation and prediction-set efficiency against a dynamically evolving benchmark for three important models. In the fully adversarial setting, exploiting the fact that the standard ACI update is exactly projected online gradient descent on the pinball loss, we derive simultaneous coverage and efficiency guarantees for arbitrary monotone Lipschitz efficiency objectives, with no distributional or convexity assumptions. In the stochastic setting with full-score feedback, we propose a sliding-window quantile tracker and establish a matching minimax lower bound showing our algorithm is rate-optimal. In the covariate-dependent stochastic setting, we develop a partitioned ACI algorithm that tracks a function-valued oracle threshold, and derive simultaneous coverage and efficiency guarantees.
notes: Alert: Lindemann. High - identifies three structural limitations of adaptive conformal inference and fixes them with online-learning guarantees

title: When Does Score Fusion Help? Conformally Certified Out-of-Distribution Detection for Camera and LiDAR Sensors
authors: Lorant Szabo, Zoltan Weltsch, Andrea Adamne-Major
matched_interests: Conformal prediction|Uncertainty quantification & failure detection for learned policies
headline: Fusing OOD detectors mostly does not help; the distribution-free FPR certificate does
summary: The authors ask when calibrated score fusion actually improves out-of-distribution detection and supply a distribution-free finite-sample false-positive-rate certificate. Four post hoc scores are calibrated to p-values by ECDF and combined by Fisher's method or cross-backbone z-score averaging, then wrapped in a conformal predictor with Hoeffding-based PAC bounds. On 215,040 PUG camera images, uniform same-backbone fusion does not beat the best single detector; the gain comes only from cross-backbone diversity, and on nuScenes LiDAR the fusion gain is small and calibration-sensitive. The PAC certificate, by contrast, transfers across both sensors with margins under 1.5%, giving evidence usable in ISO 26262 safety cases.
abstract: Camera and LiDAR sensors in safety-critical autonomous systems suffer undetected distributional shifts that silently corrupt downstream perception. Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is the established sensor-data-integrity primitive, but no single post hoc detector covers every shift type, and existing detectors lack guarantees on their false-positive rate (FPR). This paper asks when calibrated score fusion helps and provides a distribution-free finite-sample FPR certificate. Four post hoc scores - Maximum Softmax Probability (MSP), Energy, Mahalanobis distance and k-nearest-neighbour (KNN) distance - are calibrated to p-values by the empirical cumulative distribution function (ECDF) and combined by Fisher's method or cross-backbone z-score averaging, then wrapped in a conformal predictor with Hoeffding-based Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) bounds. On the full-split PUG camera benchmark (215,040 images), uniform same-backbone p-value fusion does not beat the best single detector (Mahalanobis); the gain comes from cross-backbone diversity: a z-score average of Mahalanobis distances over ResNet-50 and frozen DINOv2 reaches a mean area-under-the-ROC-curve (AUROC) of 0.9258, rising to 0.9292 with added spectral and dropout signals. On the nuScenes LiDAR sensor (256,873 frames), uniform fusion yields only a small, calibration-sensitive gain over the best single detector (MSP), so the substantial fusion gain is confined to cross-backbone averaging on the camera. The distribution-free PAC certificate, by contrast, transfers across both sensors with margins below 1.5%, giving evidence usable in ISO 26262 and EASA CoDANN safety cases.
notes: Alert: Lindemann/Tomlin. High - distribution-free FPR certificate for OOD detection that transfers across camera and LiDAR

title: Gaussian Process Conformal Prediction for Risk-Conditional Coverage Consistency
authors: Zishuo Feng, Xinyue Yan, Weibang Li
headline: Learn the miscoverage budget as a function of risk instead of one global level
summary: Most online conformal variants calibrate a single global miscoverage level for all samples, which over-covers easy cases while systematically under-covering high-risk ones when predictive risk varies. The authors learn the miscoverage budget as a continuous risk-dependent function updated online. A Gaussian-process allocation component steers calibration toward risk levels where coverage is likely to fail, while a global ACI-style correction anchors marginal coverage. The allocation component admits sublinear regret and the correction maintains O(T^-1/2) marginal deviation; across six time-series benchmarks risk-conditional coverage disparity drops without widening intervals.
abstract: Online conformal prediction gives distribution-free coverage for sequential forecasting, but many online variants calibrate one global miscoverage level for all samples. When predictive risk varies, this uniform budget can over-cover easy samples while systematically under-covering high-risk ones. We address this risk-conditional imbalance by learning the miscoverage budget as a continuous risk-dependent function and updating it online. A Gaussian-process allocation component directs calibration toward risk levels where coverage is likely to fail, while a global ACI-style correction anchors the marginal coverage level. Under the stated assumptions, the allocation component admits sublinear regret, and the correction maintains an O(T-1/2) marginal deviation. Across six time-series benchmarks, the proposed method reduces risk-conditional coverage disparity relative to strong baselines while preserving competitive interval width and accurate marginal coverage.
notes: Alert: Lindemann. Low - learns a risk-dependent miscoverage budget online, but evaluated only on time-series benchmarks [residual -1: no robotics or control component]

title: Conformal Coverage Guarantees for Any Video Temporal Grounder
authors: Aseel Mohamed, Rasul Khanbayov, Erchin Serpedin, Hasan Kurban
headline: Model-agnostic conformal wrapper turns any video grounder into one that reports coverage
summary: Independent annotators marking the same query-video pair often overlap by less than half, so the ground truth for video temporal grounding is a distribution over intervals rather than a point. COVER is a post-hoc model-agnostic wrapper turning any grounder, trained localizer or black-box video-language model, into one emitting a temporal region containing the true moment with probability at least 1-alpha. It calibrates a temporal nonconformity score quantile on held-out labels and widens the base prediction accordingly, requiring no retraining or white-box access. The authors give two score families and theory bounding certified region size and coverage under conditioning.
abstract: Event boundaries in continuous video are ambiguous: re-annotate the same query-video pair and independent annotators mark moments that overlap by less than half on a large fraction of samples. The ground truth for video temporal grounding is therefore a distribution over intervals, yet every grounder returns a single interval with no statement of reliability, so at deployment a wrong interval is indistinguishable from a right one. COVER changes the output object: a post-hoc, model-agnostic wrapper that turns any grounder, a trained localizer or a black-box video-language model, into one that emits a temporal region containing the true moment with probability at least 1-alpha, by calibrating the quantile of a temporal nonconformity score on held-out labels and widening the base prediction by that amount. The guarantee is finite-sample and distribution-free under exchangeability, and requires neither retraining nor white-box access. We give two score families, a two-sided boundary-widening score for grounders that emit an interval and a super-level-set score for grounders that emit a relevance signal, and develop theory specific to grounding that bounds how large the certified region becomes, when coverage survives conditioning on event length, and how it degrades when moments from one video break exchangeability. Across three benchmarks and five grounders, realized coverage tracks the target, and calibration exposes what point metrics hide.
notes: Alert: Lindemann. Low - model-agnostic conformal wrapper, but the application is video grounding [residual -1: vision task, no control or robotics component]

title: Adaptive Multi-Scale Forecasting and Gate-Localized Conformal Prediction for Multivariate Nonstationary Time Series
authors: Ziling Ma, Junshu Jiang, Angel Lopez-Oriona, Ying Sun, Hernando Ombao
headline: Reuse the forecaster's gate state to pick locally relevant conformal calibration residuals
summary: ABF-T-GLCP learns an adaptive predictive state representation for point forecasting and reuses it for conformal calibration. The forecasting module combines horizon-specific temporal experts through a learned gate and refines predictions using sparse predictive transfer across related series. Gate-Localized Conformal Prediction then uses that gate state, plus temporal recency, to select locally relevant calibration residuals, coupling uncertainty calibration to the predictive regimes the forecaster actually uses. On a high-frequency commodity benchmark it improves accuracy and substantially narrows intervals while keeping coverage near nominal.
abstract: We propose ABF-T-GLCP, a model-agnostic framework for forecasting and uncertainty quantification in nonstationary multivariate time series. The central idea is to learn an adaptive predictive state representation for point forecasting and reuse it for conformal calibration. The forecasting module combines horizon-specific temporal experts through a learned gate and refines predictions using sparse predictive transfer across related series. The uncertainty module, Gate-Localized Conformal Prediction (GLCP), uses the learned gate state, together with temporal recency, to select locally relevant calibration residuals, thereby coupling uncertainty calibration to the predictive regimes used by the forecasting model. This shared representation allows point forecasts and prediction intervals to adapt consistently under evolving temporal dynamics while retaining the model-agnostic nature of conformal prediction and yielding approximate local coverage under mild stability conditions. Experiments on a large-scale high-frequency commodity forecasting benchmark show consistent gains in point forecasting accuracy and substantially narrower prediction intervals with empirical coverage close to the nominal level. Additional results indicate that the framework extends beyond the motivating financial application.
notes: Alert: Lindemann. Low - couples conformal calibration to the forecaster's learned gate state [residual -1: financial time series, no robotics or control component]

title: Who Wins Where? Conformal Model Comparison for Local Superiority
authors: Yi Zhou, Baishi Li, Xuan Yao, Ke-Wei Huang
headline: Global model comparison hides which model wins where; conformal maps recover it
summary: Aggregating losses across the covariate space declares a single winner and obscures heterogeneous performance where different models are preferable in different regions. The authors introduce conformalized local model comparison, a split-sample framework building calibrated local best-model maps. Three disjoint splits fit competing models, estimate local centers and scales from out-of-sample scores, and conformally calibrate residual uncertainty, so at a target point a local winner is declared only when a one-sided conformal bound excludes a tie. They prove finite-sample marginal control on erroneous declarations and show aggregate comparison can disagree sharply with the prevalence of local superiority.
abstract: Standard model comparison is global, aggregating losses across the covariate space to declare a single winner. This can obscure heterogeneous performance, where different models are preferable in different regions. We introduce conformalized local model comparison, a split-sample framework for constructing calibrated local best-model maps. Given a model comparison score, such as the difference between two squared losses, the method uses three disjoint splits to fit competing models, estimate local centers and scales from out-of-sample scores, and conformally calibrate residual uncertainty. At a target point, the procedure declares a local winner only when a one-sided conformal bound excludes a tie, with the score's sign determining the favored model. We prove finite-sample marginal control for one-sided erroneous declarations on the realized future comparison score, establish pointwise consistency of the localized mean-score estimator away from tie boundaries, show that aggregate comparison can disagree sharply with the prevalence of local superiority, and derive a squared-loss bias-variance decomposition that clarifies how model structure affects local wins. Synthetic and real-data experiments show that the method recovers heterogeneous winner regions, abstains under uncertainty, and yields higher conditional gain than global selection.
notes: Alert: Lindemann. Low - calibrated local best-model maps, statistics-side contribution [residual -1: no robotics or control application]

title: Metriplectic Conditional Flow Matching for Structure-Preserving Dynamics Learning
authors: Ali Baheri, Lars Lindemann
headline: Flow matching that cannot inject energy, giving stable long-horizon dissipative rollouts
summary: Neural surrogates for dissipative dynamics routinely inject energy and destabilize long-horizon rollouts. MCFM instead builds the conservative-dissipative split into both the vector field parameterization and a structure-preserving sampler, training via conditional flow matching on short transitions so no long-rollout adjoints are needed. At inference a Strang-prox scheme alternates a symplectic update with a proximal metric step, ensuring discrete energy decay, with an optional projection enforcing strict decay when a trusted energy is available. On a controlled mechanical benchmark the phase portraits track ground truth more closely and energy-increase events are markedly rarer than an equally expressive unconstrained neural flow.
abstract: Metriplectic conditional flow matching (MCFM) learns dissipative dynamics without violating first principles. Neural surrogates often inject energy and destabilize long-horizon rollouts; MCFM instead builds the conservative-dissipative split into both the vector field and a structure-preserving sampler. MCFM trains via conditional flow matching on short transitions, avoiding long-rollout adjoints. In inference, a Strang-prox scheme alternates a symplectic update with a proximal metric step, ensuring discrete energy decay; an optional projection enforces strict decay when a trusted energy is available. We provide continuous and discrete-time guaranties linking this parameterization and sampler to conservation, monotonic dissipation, and stable rollouts. On a controlled mechanical benchmark, MCFM yields phase portraits closer to ground truth and markedly fewer energy-increase and positive energy-rate events than an equally expressive unconstrained neural flow, while matching terminal distributional fit.
notes: Alert: Lindemann new articles. Core - Lindemann group; builds the conservative-dissipative split into both the vector field and the sampler so rollouts cannot gain energy

title: Safe Vision Language Action Models via Barrier Enhanced Flow Matching
authors: Kasra Sinaei, Hung-Chieh Wu, Donald Ebeigbe
matched_interests: Flow matching|Control Barrier Functions (CBFs)|Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs)|Safe & robust robot control
theme_groups: Diffusion & Flow Policies|Safety & Verification|VLA & Generalist Policies
headline: Put the barrier function inside the denoiser, not as a filter on its output
summary: Rather than applying an external safety filter to a policy's final output, this framework modifies the flow matching denoising process itself so generated trajectories are inherently safe. A smooth Log-Sum-Exponential aggregate barrier enforces safety over entire action chunks with minimal computational overhead and without altering the model's semantic intent. The authors show the 2-Wasserstein distance between generated and target distributions stays bounded. The method needs no safety-specific dataset or retraining, and is validated on two robotic manipulation platforms and a 2D navigation benchmark without degrading success rate.
abstract: This article presents a modular inference framework that integrates Flow Matching generative models with formal Control Barrier Function (CBF) safety guarantees. Unlike existing methods that apply external safety filters to a model's final output, our approach modifies the Flow Matching denoising process within the model to inherently generate safe trajectories. By employing a smooth Log-Sum-Exponential aggregate barrier, we enforce safety over entire action chunks. This aggregate barrier ensures a minimal increase in computational overhead and does not alter the semantic intent of the model. We show that, within the proposed framework, the 2-Wasserstein distance between the generated distribution and the target distribution remains bounded. Our method eliminates the need for safety-specific datasets or costly model retraining, providing a versatile solution for safe inference. We validate the approach on two robotic manipulation platforms and a 2D navigation benchmark, verifying that our framework achieves reliable safety without degrading the success rate of the model.
notes: Alert: Lindemann citation. Core - CBF constraints inside the flow-matching denoising loop rather than as an external output filter

title: A Mean-Field Framework for Inference-Time Distributional Control of Diffusion Models
authors: Samuel Howard, Nikolas Nusken
headline: Steering diffusion models by distribution-level rewards, with theory instead of gradient hacks
summary: Diffusion models are increasingly steered at inference time by reward functions, but rewards defined on individual samples cannot express population-level goals like calibration or diversity. Simply adding a distributional reward gradient to the dynamics often works but carries few guarantees. The authors formulate inference-time distributional control as targeting a tilted measure under a mean-field framework and derive a weighted interacting particle scheme to hit it in a principled way. The framework recovers pointwise-reward steering as a special case and gives theoretical grounding to existing batch-level steering methods, verified in low-dimensional settings and on protein conformation tasks.
abstract: Diffusion models are increasingly used as controllable samplers, whose generations can be steered at inference time according to a chosen reward function. While such rewards are typically defined on individual samples, for many applications it is desirable to steer according to distribution-level rewards, for example to calibrate with population-level information or to encourage diversity. In both cases, simply incorporating the reward gradient into the dynamics, while often effective, comes with few theoretical guarantees on the sampled distribution. For pointwise rewards, recent work has therefore sought to develop a principled framework for targeting a prescribed tilted distribution using particle reweighting. However, an analogous theoretically-grounded approach for distributional rewards is currently lacking. In this work, we formulate inference-time distributional control as targeting a tilted measure under a mean-field framework, and derive a weighted interacting particle scheme to target it in a principled manner. Our framework recovers pointwise-reward steering as a special case, while providing a theoretical foundation for existing batch-level steering methods. Empirically, we verify that the procedure correctly targets the prescribed distribution in tractable low-dimensional settings, and investigate its behaviour in higher-dimensional protein conformation tasks.
notes: Alert: Fan citation. Core - principled particle scheme for steering diffusion samplers by distribution-level rather than pointwise rewards

title: PAC-DP: PAC-Bayesian Diffusion Policy Learning
authors: Mohammad Hasan Yeganegi, Dian Yu, Andrea Del Prete, Majid Khadiv, Matteo Saveriano
headline: A PAC-Bayes generalization bound becomes the diffusion policy training objective
summary: Diffusion policies are trained by minimizing a denoising objective that offers little control over generalization in the small-data regimes typical of robotics. The authors model the diffusion policy as a Bayesian neural network, define a PAC-Bayes generalization bound, and derive a training objective augmenting the denoising loss with a KL regularizer between posterior and prior parameter distributions. This is a principled way to regularize training without meaningfully increasing training time. Experiments show better denoising, lower variational negative log-likelihood, and higher success rates across manipulation benchmarks, with the largest gains in low-data regimes and complex tasks.
abstract: Diffusion Policies (DPs) are able to perform complex manipulation tasks. However, DPs are typically trained by minimizing a denoising objective, which provides limited control over generalization in the finite-data regimes common in robotics. In this letter, we propose PAC-DP, an approach that increases the performance of DPs in robotic manipulation tasks. By modeling the DP as a Bayesian neural network, and defining a PAC-Bayes generalization bound, we derive a novel training objective that augments the standard denoising loss with a Kullback-Leibler divergence regularizer between the posterior and prior parameter distributions. From the theoretical perspective, our approach provides a principled approach to regularize the training of DPs without significantly increasing the training time. From the practical point of view, experimental results demonstrate improved denoising performance, lower variational negative log-likelihood, and higher success rates across multiple robotic manipulation benchmarks. Crucially, the largest improvements are observed in low-data training regimes and complex tasks, establishing PAC-DP as a theoretically grounded framework for robot policy learning.
notes: Alert: Bajcsy/Majumdar citation. Core - turns a PAC-Bayes generalization bound into the training objective for diffusion policies

title: Latent MeanFlow Policy Optimization for Offline Reinforcement Learning
authors: Tenglong Liu, Xin Xu, Yixing Lan, Jiacheng Huang, Xinglong Zhang, Ling-Li Zeng
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
headline: One-step MeanFlow action generation replaces iterative sampling in offline RL
summary: Diffusion and flow-matching policies improve expressiveness in offline RL but pay for it with multi-step sampling and uninformative Gaussian priors. LaMPO learns a behavior-conditioned latent distribution that supplies an informative prior and reduces the generative modeling burden. Conditioned on that prior, a MeanFlow policy predicts average action velocity for high-fidelity one-step action generation, and the target policy is optimized under a MeanFlow-induced behavior constraint with a proven performance lower bound. Across 71 tasks in OGBench, D4RL, and real humanoid manipulation it delivers a 19% average improvement and 81% real-world success.
abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) aims to derive effective policies from fixed datasets without environment interaction.
